children.text: granthaprastāvanā: mokṣa-sādhanarūpa se dharma kī upādeyatā
children.translated_text: Introduction: The worthiness of Dharma as the means of liberation
Having bowed to the Supreme Self (<s>Paramātman</s>),
I shall declare, out of desire for the benefit
of beings of limited understanding,
a compendium of the discourses of the sciences (<s>Śāstravārttāsamuccaya</s>).
Hearing which, in all the sciences,
generally, a determination of the truth
arises, one that pacifies hatred,
and brings the happiness of heavenly accomplishment.
Suffering comes from sin, happiness from <s>Dharma</s>—
this is established in all the sciences.
Therefore sin should not be committed,
and an accumulation of <s>Dharma</s> should be made.
The five—violence (<s>hiṃsā</s>), falsehood, and the rest—
and also disbelief in the truths (<s>tattvas</s>),
and the four beginning with anger—
these are the causes of sin.
But the opposites of these are the causes of <s>Dharma</s>,
as declared by the wise;
constant effort in these
should be properly made by one who seeks happiness.
Service of the virtuous always with devotion,
<s>maitrī</s> (loving-kindness) toward beings with genuine feeling,
and release from the grip of egoism—
these are the means of establishing the cause of <s>Dharma</s>.
Constant good instruction,
the sight of practitioners of <s>Dharma</s>,
and discipline in the proper place—this is
the great fruit of service to the virtuous.
For one who constantly cultivates <s>maitrī</s>,
a virtuous disposition arises;
from the arising of that disposition in a being,
the fire of hatred subsides.
The generator of all faults,
the destroyer of all virtues—
through release from the grip of egoism,
even craving (<s>tṛṣṇā</s>) is turned back.
Thus, endowed with a host of virtues,
of purified soul, of steady disposition,
he is declared to be one who has understood the truths (<s>tattvas</s>),
a proper practitioner of <s>Dharma</s>.
And what is to be adopted in <s>saṃsāra</s>
is <s>Dharma</s> alone, as always stated by the wise;
the pure <s>Dharma</s> is for liberation; everything
else is the cause of suffering.
The union with the beloved is impermanent,
here it is dear to jealousy and grief;
youth too is impermanent,
the ground for despicable conduct.
Possessions are impermanent,
produced from the group of intense afflictions;
and life here is impermanent,
the bond of all states of existence.
Again birth, again death,
taking refuge in low and other stations;
and again and again, therefore
happiness is not found here.
For everything in <s>saṃsāra</s> is thus
inherently unbeautiful;
therefore, tell me, is any attachment
fitting for the discerning?
Except <s>Dharma</s>, worthy of the world's homage,
stainless, eternal,
accomplishing the welfare of others,
practiced by the steadfast who possess good character—
one says that even in <s>Dharma</s>, attachment is not fitting
if examined correctly,
because even the auspicious result of <s>Dharma</s>
is considered to be bondage itself.
And between a bond of iron
and one of gold,
there is no difference in the result,
since there is no difference in servitude.
Therefore, like <s>adharma</s>, <s>Dharma</s> too
should be abandoned by seekers of liberation;
for liberation through the destruction of both <s>Dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>
has been described by the sages.
It is replied: That is indeed so,
but <s>Dharma</s> is considered twofold:
one is the yoga of knowledge (<s>jñānayoga</s>),
and the other has the mark of merit (<s>puṇya</s>).
The yoga of knowledge is pure austerity,
free from the fault of expectation;
through the excellence of practice, it is declared
to be the means of liberation.
If that is truly <s>Dharma</s>,
why does it not have bondage as its fruit?
If another, also free from expectation,

children.text: kiṃ naivaṃ ced na yat tathā
children.translated_text: why is it not so? Because it is not of that nature.
<s>Dharma</s> whose fruits are enjoyment and liberation
is of the nature of both activity and its opposite;
and has the form of right and wrong and the rest;
such is the course even in other systems.
But without that <s>Dharma</s>,
how is the destruction of both achieved?
It would always exist or never exist,
if it were truly without cause.
Therefore, some cause for the destruction of both
must necessarily be sought;
that very thing is to be known as <s>Dharma</s>,
the pure one that bestows the fruit of liberation.
Liberation through the destruction of <s>Dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>—
and what was said about the mark of merit—
that <s>Dharma</s> is to be abandoned, depending on that context,
but not the one that is the yoga of knowledge.
Therefore attachment is fitting in that very one,
if examined correctly;
everything else in <s>saṃsāra</s>
has been shown to be the cause of suffering.
And from that, liberation arises,
free from death and the rest—
this we shall explain later
in accordance with the correct sciences.
Now, in brief,
the correctness of the science is stated
through the refutation of the false reasoning
of bad doctrines, without contradiction.
(2) Refutation of the doctrine of consciousness arising from elements (<s>Bhūtacaitanyavāda</s>)
This world is merely the effect
of the great elements beginning with earth;
and the proponents of the element doctrine
do not consider the self to have established existence.
The elements are non-conscious;
consciousness is neither their property nor their effect.
Others say: that in which
consciousness exists—that alone is the self.
If consciousness were a property of the elements,
it would be perceived individually in each of them at all times,
like sentience and other qualities,
just as hardness and the rest.
It does not exist in them in the form of a potency,
and therefore it is not perceived;
nor in that form either,
if it is both existent and non-existent—that is not valid.
Of potency and consciousness,
there is either identity or difference in every respect;
if identical, then it is consciousness itself;
if different, then it belongs to another.
The non-manifestation of this
is also not logically established,
since there is no obstruction by another,
because that would contradict the enumeration of the truths.
And it is not obstructed by their own nature
or by any one of them,
because of the assertion of a manifester;
for that which is obstructed is not a manifester.
Even in the case of a special transformation,
obstruction is not valid here,
because then, by the attainment of existence,
the consequence of being a manifester would follow.
And since it is not different from the elements,
manifestation would always occur;
but if different, with additional existence,
the enumeration of the truths would not be valid.
If it is said that at its own time it is non-different—
in the absence of time, that is not valid;
but as for the self, based on what is established in the world—
alas! How is it not resorted to?
The self too is not established in the world
merely from the memory of past births,
since the absence of that in all
is due to the ripening of varied <s>karmas</s>.
In the world too, it is observed that those who come
from a single place
do not all equally have
the remembrance of experienced objects.
And from divine vision,
from the non-deviation of the tradition of the learned,
and from the establishment of rites for ancestors and the like—
alas! The self is indeed not worldly.
Hardness and non-cognition are the nature
of the elements, as established by perception;
consciousness is not of that nature—
how then could it be their effect?
Being absent in each of them individually,
it could not be like atoms and oil;
if present, it would be perceived
in all, which are of distinct natures, at all times.
Just as bulk, which is absent in atoms and the like,
is seen in pots and the like—
so too, though absent in the elements,
consciousness also—if such is the thought—
bulk is not absent in atoms and the like,
since it arises from them alone;
the production of what is non-existent from them
is not valid, due to the fallacy of over-extension.
A fifth element too,
since there is no difference in non-existence from those—
its production would follow; and thus
the enumeration of the truths would not be valid.
If they do not have the nature of producing it—
there is no evidence for that here;
if the production of bulk is accepted,
that would be the same even in its existence.
And bulk is not something different
from the aggregate of material atoms;
the state of those being such
is proper, without contradiction with evidence.
If different, since it is insufficient thereby—
how does it attain existence?
Even in its absence, if it existed,
it would be everywhere and always.
And it is not accepted that consciousness
is merely an aggregate of elements;
since its existence would equally follow
without distinction everywhere.
This being so, pots and the like,
having manifest consciousness,
would not differ from persons—
and that is contradicted by perception.
If elements of different natures
produce consciousness here and there in their aggregates—
this too is not valid,
since it is not in all aggregates.
The inherent nature, when merely elemental,
does not differ by logic,
since without a differentiating factor,
there is no distinction among equals.
And if the difference is only in inherent form,
the distinction would be of a non-elemental nature;
but in the existence of a differentiating factor,
that very thing would be the self.
Oblation, preparations of jaggery and grain flour,
and other things produced from the aggregate of substances
are of different natures;
like edible things—if this is the objection,
their difference in nature
is only in their manifest form;
no difference in the effect of taste, potency, ripening, etc.
is found.
If being merely of that nature,
this distinction in configuration and the rest
exists among the elements—
why should not that too exist?
Because there is no agent; and because of the non-applicability
of difference in place, time, etc.;
and this is not unestablished, since if merely elemental,
it would be impossible.
And being merely elemental,
no distinction between aggregate and non-aggregate
is valid, due to the absence of a differentiator—
let this be properly considered.
That 'this is one, that is another'—
if merely of that nature, such a distinction
does not hold, since that too is not different;
therefore the two are equal.
This may be so—even if produced from elements,
the variety of stones and the like
is established in the world—this is indeed established;
but that is not produced from them alone.
Because it arises from the totality of causes including
the unseen (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>), space, time, and the rest;
likewise, from worldly knowledge;
otherwise, from the absence of that.
And the worldly path
is not what is being examined by us here;
but where does this apply?—and your doctrine
has not stated that.
And in a dead body, consciousness
would be perceived in every case,
as being a property of the body and the like—
that is a property of those, and not otherwise.
And there is no deviation through
beauty, hardness, and dark color,
since they exist even in a dead body—
this accords with perception itself.
If beauty does not exist—
then that is not caused by those elements alone;
precisely because of the existence of another—
it is established that the self exists.
The vital breaths and the like are not the evidence;
why? Because even in their existence there is equality;
if their absence means non-existence,
then in the absence of the self—what is the evidence?
Therefore, the existence of those being conditioned by that—
it is not again established by bellows and the like;
even if that were established—
if it is said 'that is something else'—that is not so.
If it is said that from the general establishment of wind,
that is its nature—not so;
your evidence here too, if it is only
the production of consciousness—
there is doubt in that very thing;
if asked, 'why is this not yours?'—
by the existence of the nature of each—
if asked, 'how is there absence of that?'—
from the perception of their distinctness—
for this arises from the consciousness of the mother;
in that son, there would be no fault—
it is not that it does not exist in his mother.
And in sweat-born and other beings,
it would not exist by the absence of a mother;
what is known by the lamp analogy here
is not an objection, since it is merely instrumental.
Thus, the elements are not established
as the material cause of consciousness in any way;
and in the absence of any other material cause,
that very thing must be the self.
Nothing arises without
a cause that has such a nature;
and nothing perishes absolutely—
as the great sage <s>Vyāsa</s> has said:
"Of the non-existent, there is no coming into being;
of the existent, there is no ceasing to be;
the conclusion regarding both of these
has been seen by the seers of truth."
Non-existence does not attain existence,
as in the case of hare's horns;
existence does not attain non-existence here—
if a lamp does, that is not so in every respect.
Thus, the self, possessing consciousness,
is established from its perpetual existence;
it should be known even in the next world
by those who follow the path of reasoning.

children.text: (3)maiṃ viṣayaka pratyakṣa anubhava se ātmā kī siddhi
children.translated_text: (3) Proof of the self through the direct perceptual experience relating to 'I'
If the self exists, why, like a pot,
is it not perceived through perception?
There is indeed clear perception of it,
from the experience of the 'I'-cognition.
'I am deluded,' 'I am heavy'—this
is true; but that is considered to be of another;
because of its erring nature,
it is said not to be indicative.
That objection applies to perception too,
since there is no difference in their existence;
if the other is a semblance of perception
that errs—that is not correct.
In the view of the 'I'-cognition too,
all this is the same;
therefore, like that, let this primary
perception be accepted as valid.
'My body is heavy'—from the observation
of differentiated cognition in such cases,
the nature of being deluded
is proper for that considered deluded, but not for the other.
The self's apprehension of the self too
is established from experience;
since that is of that very nature,
it is not that it is not established by reasoning.
And this ego-sense (<s>ahaṃkāra</s>) is not conceived
as a special modification of the intellect,
because even at the time of cognitions such as giving,
the experience of ego-sense is present.
The self's non-apprehension of the self,
given that it is of that very nature—
its perpetual non-apprehension
should be known as due to the fault of <s>karma</s>.
Therefore, established through direct perception
for all living beings,
this self is self-luminous—always;
so it is read in the <s>Veda</s> too.

children.text: (4) ātmā tathā karma ke sambandha meṃ matamatāntara
children.translated_text: (4) Differences of opinion regarding the relationship between the self and karma
Here too, some explain—
the Buddhists who have attained understanding—
the mind that is afflicted exists eternally;
that has the characteristics of the self as stated.
If it is eternal, then it is itself the self,
the difference being merely in designation;
but if it is non-eternal, then this
does not have the characteristics of the self as stated.
He who is the agent of the distinctions of action,
the experiencer of the fruits of action,
the transmigrator, the one who attains complete <s>Nirvāṇa</s>—
he indeed is the <s>Ātman</s> (self), having no other characteristic.
The diversity of that which is undifferentiated in being the self,
on account of which it takes forms such as human—
that variegated [factor] is called
<s>adṛṣṭa</s> (the unseen), designated as <s>karma</s>.
Likewise, even when effort is equal
and the means are good, the difference in results among men
cannot be explained
by reasoning without another cause.
Therefore, another cause must necessarily be accepted
there by others;
that very thing is called <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (the unseen)
by others who have labored in the scriptures.
Since beings have that as their nature,
even this is an unsurpassed [answer];
that the self is not merely elemental—
this has been demonstrated here.
Since <s>karma</s> is of a material nature,
even this is the present [view]:
it is distinct from the self,
since it is considered to have a variegated nature.
Others, however, the learned, declare
that it has the form of a potency (<s>śakti</s>);
yet others consider it to have the form
of an impression (<s>vāsanā</s>), yielding diverse fruits.
Others, however, state here:
for an agent whose nature is fixed,
without connection with something else,
how can there be a spontaneous potency?
If that [potency] arises from the conjunction with action,
then it is not tenable when that [action] is not nourished;
and in the absence of conjunction with something other than that,
how can there be nourishment of it?
It exists always indeed, but
it is merely manifested by action;
[reply:] of that which resides in the self alone,
there is never any manifestation.
In the absence of obstruction by something other than it,
its very existence would be its activity;
manifestation through the removal of that [obstruction]—
such is the arrangement of its divisions.
Let the sin, being different, be
caused by another kind of action;
in that case, why is merit, produced by desired action,
not similarly regarded?
<s>Vāsanā</s> (impression) too, without connection with something else,
is simply not tenable;
for in the absence of fragrance from flowers and the like,
it is not observed in sesame seeds, etc.
Let some substratum be accepted
that is distinct from mere consciousness;
that itself is your primary <s>karma</s>—
<s>vāsanā</s> otherwise is not appropriate.
If, in the case of mere consciousness,
no knowledge is free from impressions,
then there would always be non-liberation,
and no distinctiveness of the pure [consciousness].
Thus, the thesis of potency (<s>śakti</s>) and the like
does not work, due to fallacies;
from bondage being deficient or excessive,
but it is tenable due to the existence of that [karmic matter].
Therefore, <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (the unseen) must be understood
as distinct from the self, variegated,
connected with the self,
and as the accomplisher of potency and the rest.
<s>Adṛṣṭa</s>, <s>karma</s>, <s>saṃskāras</s> (impressions),
merit and demerit, auspicious and inauspicious,
<s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, and likewise <s>pāśa</s> (bond)—
these are declared as its synonyms.
Its causes have been stated:
violence, falsehood, and the like, as before;
one who possesses these is conjoined with that [karma],
which yields diverse fruits.
Since there is no contradiction with perception or inference,
and its establishment is unobstructed,
the learned declare this very [doctrine]
to be the teaching of reality.
(5) Refutation of the doctrine that consciousness arises from elements, and conclusion
The doctrine of the <s>Lokāyatas</s> (materialists) should be known by the wise
as the cause of a flood of sin;
being contrary to truth in this way,
it does not foster knowledge.
<s>Bṛhaspati</s> is said to have composed this
for the deception of <s>Indra</s>;
but even that is devoid of reasoning, since
<s>Indra</s> would not be deceived in this manner.
Therefore, the <s>Nāstika</s> (nihilist) view,
which produces corrupt dispositions,
conceived by beings afflicted with defilements,
and of evil repute, should always be rejected by the wise.
Second Section

children.text: (2)puṇya, pāpa tathā mokṣa se saṃbaṃdhita kuccha praśna
children.translated_text: (2) Some questions related to merit, sin, and liberation
From violence and the like, inauspicious <s>karma</s> arises,
and from other [actions], auspicious [karma];
this regularity is derived from authoritative testimony—
"from where else?" say others.
Others say, from scripture (<s>āgama</s>);
and that is not contradicted by perception and the rest;
it has all objects as its scope, is eternal,
has clear meaning, and is composed by the Supreme Self.
From the observation of concordance
regarding eclipses of the sun and moon and the like,
even regarding sin and such, which are imperceptible,
its authoritativeness is not untenable.
Even if concordance is sometimes observed
regarding one thing or another,
how is the existence or the true nature of that
to be ascertained?
From the unity of the scriptures,
from the similarity of statements and the like,
from the well-established tradition,
and also from the diminution of sin.
Otherwise, investigation of the true nature of things
would simply not be possible,
since doubt is all-pervading
and arises in one who uses deception.
Non-investigation too is not appropriate,
because of the non-discrimination of qualities and defects;
I suspect a great difficulty has arisen
for the exponents of reasoning.
Therefore, from the authoritative testimony
of scripture as stated, properly,
that inauspicious results arise from violence and the like—
this regularity is established.
From the afflicted performance of violence and the like,
afflicted <s>karma</s> is obtained,
as disease [comes] to one who eats unwholesome food;
the opposite comes from the reverse.
This is the nature of the <s>jīva</s> (soul):
that it undergoes such transformations;
it is bound by merit and demerit,
but is liberated through equanimity (<s>mādhyasthya</s>).
Even having gone very far in this matter,
among the established explanations,
who, at the conclusion of [investigating] nature and scripture,
would not take refuge?
Through the nature of the antidote
and through the scripture of the antidote,
since these are refuted—how then can these two
be the refuge of exponents of reasoning?
That which is refuted by dependent [reasoning]—
that nature is not tenable for a thing,
even if hypothesized,
like coldness of fire, etc.
"Fire does indeed have coldness—
why is its effect not observed?"
[Reply:] "It is observed near ice;
how is this so by its nature?"
"Even ice has this nature:
necessarily, in the proximity of fire,
it produces burning"—in that case,
would fire not have coldness?
Due to the absence of a fixed rule, thus,
your understanding here being of such kind,
that [understanding] would make the effect of a clod
attributable to you, by its nature.
Thus, the absence of good understanding
would follow for you as well;
if it is so, then we have no dispute
with one entirely devoid of understanding.
Another says: even if it is established that
from violence and the like comes inauspicious [karma] and the rest,
that happiness comes from auspicious [karma] alone—
by what means of knowledge is this known?
Here too, some say,
the thoroughgoing exponents of reasoning:
this is ascertained by reasoning
that is pregnant with observation.
By that, they say: happiness does not come from the inauspicious,
because of the consequent abundance of it;
for those who do sinful deeds are many,
while those who do good are rare.
And this is not seen in the world,
since an abundance of suffering is observed;
therefore, happiness from the auspicious is established,
and so on, from these considerations.
Others, however, the faithful,
say this by scripture:
happiness comes from the auspicious alone,
and is never known from any other source.
In matters that are beyond the senses,
mostly of this kind,
for one who uses deception, there is no means of knowledge
that is free from error.
And what was said about the observation
of an abundance of suffering—that is not a proof;
for even if it is sometimes observed,
it is not seen everywhere, thus [the argument fails].
"But one for whom it is seen everywhere—
why is his statement not a proof?"
[Reply:] That statement is indeed a proof,
but then it does not differ from scripture.
The occasional attainment of happiness
even from the performance of the inauspicious—
that is the fruit, devoid of the flavor of ripening,
of such [previously earned] <s>karma</s>.
From the performance following the instruction
regarding the slaying of a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>, the acquisition of a village, etc.—
this is not from that [act] itself;
this is known from scripture alone.
And of the opposing scriptures,
because of contradiction with perception and inference,
and because of being composed by non-authoritative persons,
the status of [valid] scripture is not tenable.
And the contradiction with perception and inference
establishes that they are not composed by authoritative persons;
since this is necessarily known,
let that very [point] be demonstrated.
The statement that approaching forbidden women and the like
is a means of <s>dharma</s> in some cases
contradicts well-known
direct perception.
And liberation is accepted
through the excellence of one's own <s>dharma</s> alone;
its existence due to the absence of a cause
is contradicted by the accepted [fact of] permanence.
Equanimity (<s>mādhyasthya</s>) alone is its cause;
through approaching forbidden women and the like
that supreme [equanimity] is accomplished—
therefore there is no fault in that.
This too is mere assertion; in activities
such as approaching forbidden women,
equanimity is not tenable
by reasoning, given such engagement.
Through non-engagement everywhere,
according to the extent of one's capacity,
through the practice of pure contemplation—
that supreme equanimity arises.
As long as such [pure contemplation] does not arise,
whatever engagement there is
is specially good, since
it furthers the excellence of that [equanimity].
It is not the cause of non-engagement,
since it does not turn one back from something;
since the stream of states is unbroken everywhere,
otherwise there would be the status of the unfathomable.
Let that be as stated in the worldly and scriptural traditions;
from the conjunction of indifference in that regard,
this supreme [equanimity] is possible indeed
for the purification of the dispositions of great souls.
Even for one who liberates from <s>saṃsāra</s> (transmigration),
if violence is a means of <s>dharma</s>,
and there is liberation thereby—then for him too
this fault is unresolved.
Liberation arises from the destruction of <s>karma</s> alone,
never from anything else;
since it is devoid of birth and the rest—
this very [point] is to be examined here.
Is the destruction of <s>karma</s> accomplished through
the excellence of violence and the like, or through their opposite,
or through another cause, or without cause at all?
This must be considered.
If accomplished through the excellence of violence and the like,
then in its absence, it would not persist;
and if the destruction of <s>karma</s> does not persist,
there would be the impermanence of the liberation of the liberated.
If accomplished through the opposite [of violence],
that is the position of the other [Jain] doctrine;
for the destruction of <s>karma</s>, according to the virtuous,
is accomplished through non-violence and the like.
If accomplished through another cause,
the nature of that [cause] is not established;
if without cause, then it would either always exist
or never exist at all.
Liberation is accepted as arising from the destruction of <s>karma</s>,
and that is the fruit of the practice of knowledge;
and non-violence and the like are its cause—
this is the reasoning accepted by the virtuous.
Thus, even violence enjoined by the <s>Vedas</s>
is truly conducive to downfall;
even when enjoined by scripture,
it is contradicted by other statements.
"One should not harm living beings here;
harming is considered to produce fault"—
this is clear, like cauterization in medicine,
from the general rule and its exception.
"Cauterization should be performed
when enjoined for the cure of disease"—
even from that, there is fault nonetheless,
since the injunction is for the sake of a result.
Thus, even when there is that result,
and even from the injunction in every way,
the fault arising from the general rule
certainly arises, due to the injunction for a result.
For the doctrines of others too,
the contradiction with perception and inference
through such reasoning should be demonstrated—
[regarding] false scriptures; and thus that is established.
The afflicted performance of violence and the like—
if it did not arise from anything other [than the self],
then the self alone would be the agent
of all action indeed.
Due to beginningless connection with <s>karma</s>,
from delusion regarding that, one engages
even in what is harmful to oneself, for the most part,
like one whose mind is afflicted by disease.
(1) The doctrines of Time, Nature, Fate, Karma, and the combination of Time and other factors
Others, the proponents, consider
Time and the rest to be the agent;
yet others [consider] each alone,
while others [consider them] in mutual combination.
Without Time, no fetal [development],
childhood, auspiciousness, and the like—
whatever arises in the world—
that [Time] is said to be the cause.
"Time ripens beings,
Time destroys creatures,
Time is awake when [all] are asleep,
Time is indeed hard to overcome."
Moreover, without Time,
even the cooking of mung beans is not accepted,
even in the presence of pot and the rest;
therefore that [cooking] is considered to be from Time.
And in the absence of Time, fetal [development] and the rest—
all would be without regularity,
since they would arise merely from the existence
of the causes accepted by others.
Without Nature (<s>svabhāva</s>), no fetal [development],
childhood, auspiciousness, and the like—
whatever arises in the world—
that [Nature] is said to be the cause.
All things, by their own nature,
each in its own nature, in various ways,
arise and cease,
averse to arbitrary action.
Without Nature,
even the cooking of mung beans is not accepted;
likewise, even in the presence of Time and the rest,
that [cooking] does not apply to horse-beans, since [they lack the nature].
In the absence of that nature, if that [result] exists,
the undesirable over-extension is unresolved;
in that case, equally, a pot from clay
but not cloth and the rest—that is irrational.
Since all things arise
in a fixed form,
they are born of Fate (<s>niyati</s>),
due to conformity with the nature of that [Fate].
Whatever arises, whenever, from whatever, to whatever extent—
that very thing arises then, from that, in that way,
necessarily, by logic—
who is able to refute this?
Without Fate, in the world,
even the cooking of mung beans is not observed.
Even when its inherent nature and so forth exist,
since it is not fixed,
if it were otherwise unfixed,
the existence of everything would follow absurdly,
because of the absurd consequence of mutual identity,
and actions would become fruitless.
There is no object of enjoyment in the world
apart from the enjoyer;
and there can be no enjoyment of what is not produced,
since for the liberated, enjoyment does not exist.
And the entire world is the object of enjoyment for beings;
that which is seen by this or that means,
is directly perceived —
therefore it is born of <s>karma</s> (action).
And in the absence of <s>karma</s>,
even the cooking of lentils is not observed,
since, due to the breaking of pots and so forth,
it does not occur in some cases.
Diverse enjoyment arises from diverse <s>karma</s>;
otherwise, there would be no causation,
since its diversity
cannot be accounted for by <s>niyati</s> (fate) and the like.
Since <s>niyati</s> is of fixed nature,
there would be sameness for all fixed things;
and if its nature were unfixed,
its diversity would arise only by force.
And the diversity of this
cannot be accounted for merely by the nature of the <s>tanmātras</s> (subtle elements) and the like,
except by positing a differentiating factor other than that,
in accordance with correct reasoning without contradiction.
Water, being of one form,
does not acquire diversity from merely falling from the sky,
without the differentiating factor
of saline and other types of earth.
And if that differentiation is caused by something distinct from it,
then that is not the agent of it;
and if it is the agent, then its diversity too
is similarly untenable.
If such is claimed to be
the inherent nature of <s>niyati</s> itself,
then the doctrine of <s>niyati</s> (fate) would be abandoned
in favor of resorting to <s>svabhāva</s> (inherent nature), would it not?
And one's own existence is indeed one's inherent nature,
for it is nothing but one's own being;
in the absence of a differentiating factor for that too,
diversity cannot be accounted for.
Therefore, due to its undifferentiated nature,
the simultaneous arising of everything would follow;
and since this is not the case, by sound reasoning
the doctrine of <s>svabhāva</s> too is not tenable.
If that universal cause is dependent on
particular times and so forth, then surely
the doctrine of <s>svabhāva</s> would be abandoned
in favor of adopting the doctrine of <s>kāla</s> (time).
And if <s>kāla</s> (time), in the sense of 'occasion' and the like,
is itself the sole cause,
even that is not tenable,
since some things do not arise from time alone.
And therefore, even when time is equal,
the same result does not occur everywhere;
hence it should be understood by the discerning
that it depends on other causes.
Therefore, time and all the others
are causes collectively,
of effects such as the embryo and the like —
this should be understood by those who argue according to reason.
And nowhere in this world
is anything observed to arise from a single cause alone;
therefore, the aggregate of conditions (<s>sāmagrī</s>)
is held to be the producer of every effect.
Some declare <s>svabhāva</s> (inherent nature) and <s>niyati</s> (fate)
to be other than <s>karma</s>;
but others hold that <s>dharma</s>
applies to all things universally.
Third Cluster.
(1) Refutation of the Doctrine of <s>Īśvara</s> (God as Creator).
<s>Īśvara</s> (God) is held by some to be the creator
in the role of an instigator here;
endowed with inconceivable conscious power,
eternally pure — so say the learned ones.
His knowledge is unobstructed,
and the Lord of the world possesses <s>vairāgya</s> (dispassion),
sovereignty, and <s>dharma</s> —
a fourfold set inherently accomplished.
"This ignorant creature, powerless
over its own happiness and suffering,
impelled by <s>Īśvara</s>, goes
either to heaven or to the abyss."
Others, however, state here:
"Since the <s>Vītarāga</s> (passionless one) is of such a nature,
in the absence of any purpose,
how can creatorship be justified?
For what reason does he impel
some creatures to actions leading to hell
and others to actions leading to heaven
swiftly?
If beings engage in diverse actions
of their own accord,
why is the creatorship of <s>Īśvara</s>
proclaimed here to be purposeless?
If he gives all the results
because he has instigated the actions,
in the absence of results, the earlier fault applies;
when results exist, it is mere devotion."
Even for the initial creation, there is no cause
for one whose purpose is already accomplished;
and since it contradicts the thesis,
<s>svabhāva</s> (inherent nature) too is without authority.
If <s>karma</s> and the like are of his inherent nature,
nothing contradicts the Lord's nature;
but if the Lord is of such inherent nature,
there is contradiction with his being one whose purpose is accomplished.
Therefore, this doctrine of <s>Īśvara</s>'s creatorship
is justified only
in accordance with correct reasoning without contradiction,
as those of pure understanding have said.
<s>Īśvara</s> is indeed the <s>Paramātman</s> (Supreme Self);
from the practice of the vows he has prescribed,
liberation comes; therefore, his being the agent
of that would follow from the nature of his qualities.
Since <s>saṃsāra</s> (cycle of existence) truly results
from the non-practice of that,
therefore, his being the agent of that too,
when conceived thus, is not faulty.
Since some have reverence because his word says
"He is the creator,"
therefore, in conformity with that,
his creatorship is taught.
Since the <s>Ātman</s> (Self) is endowed with supreme sovereignty,
the Self itself is regarded as <s>Īśvara</s>;
and saying "He is the creator" is faultless —
the doctrine of creatorship thus stands established.
The authors of the <s>śāstras</s> (treatises) are great souls,
generally free from desire for worldly existence,
and engaged in the welfare of beings —
how could they speak what is unjust?
Therefore, their intention should be
properly sought by one who desires their welfare,
in accordance with the science of logic,
as <s>Manu</s> too has said:
"The revealed <s>dharmaśāstra</s> (code of law),
he who investigates with reasoning
that does not contradict the Vedic sciences,
he knows <s>Dharma</s> — not another."
(2) Refutation of the Doctrine of <s>Prakṛti</s> (Primordial Nature) and <s>Puruṣa</s> (Spirit).
Others consider that everything arises
from <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial matter);
in the order of <s>Mahat</s> (great intellect) and so forth,
the wise ones hold this class of effects arises here.
From <s>Pradhāna</s> arises <s>Mahat</s>,
and from that, <s>Ahaṃkāra</s> (ego-sense),
and from that, the group of sense-organs and <s>tanmātras</s> (subtle elements),
and from the <s>tanmātras</s>, the aggregate of gross elements.
Pots and the like arise from the transformation
of earth and other elements;
nothing in the world is produced
by the activity of the <s>Ātman</s> (Self).
Others, however, say that this is merely
a description of the cosmogonic procedure;
without examining it by reason,
it is accepted on faith alone, supremely.
But by reason it is contradicted, since
<s>Pradhāna</s> is held to be eternal;
if it does not deviate from its own nature,
how can <s>Mahat</s> and the rest arise from it?
If it is said, "Because such is its inherent nature" —
then why not always?
If one says "For that very reason" —
then, it being of such nature, whence does that come?
Without a material cause, one thing
never comes into being from another;
and if it is a material cause,
then it is not absolutely eternal.
Even pots and the like are observed to arise
dependent on potters and such;
therefore, they do not arise
from the mere transformation of earth and the like.
If the body is the agent there,
it is not truly separate from the <s>Ātman</s>;
but if it is indeed separate,
how is enjoyment of the <s>Ātman</s> justified?
It is not held that the <s>Ātman</s>'s enjoyment
consists of the body's enjoyment;
rather, it is through the arising of a reflection,
as the earlier masters have said:
"The <s>Puruṣa</s> (Spirit), whose nature is unmodified,
by its mere proximity makes the unconscious
mind, which is self-luminous,
its support — just as a crystal does.
When the intellect is transformed into the semblance of the seer,
his enjoyment is spoken of;
it is the arising of a reflection, as of the moon
in clear water."
But even this arising of a reflection
is not justified for something that is incorporeal;
and due to the absurd consequence regarding the liberated,
enjoyment never truly exists.
Nor is it inapplicable to the liberated
because of its being their previous nature;
and if there is a change of nature,
transformation is not prevented.
Since the <s>Ātman</s> is separate from the body,
acts of violence and the like do not apply to it anywhere;
and in the absence of those, since there is no cause,
how can there be auspicious or inauspicious bondage?
Without bondage, neither <s>saṃsāra</s>
nor liberation of the <s>Ātman</s> is possible;
and in the absence of those,
<s>yama</s> (restraints) and all else would be entirely purposeless.
"The <s>Ātman</s> is neither bound
nor ever liberated;
it is <s>Prakṛti</s> (Nature) that is bound
and liberated by its own self" — if this is claimed,
for that which is absolutely of one form
and eternal, in no way whatsoever,
due to the absence of any different activity,
can bondage and liberation be justified by reason.
If liberation is the disjunction of <s>Prakṛti</s>,
how can it be hers?
For there would be the absurd consequence of the loss of her essential nature,
and also contradiction with the doctrine.
"One who knows the twenty-five <s>tattvas</s> (principles),
devoted to whatever <s>āśrama</s> (stage of life),
whether wearing matted hair, shaven, or with a topknot,
is liberated — there is no doubt here" —
thus liberation of the <s>Puruṣa</s>
has been declared in the doctrine by the ancients;
but this does not hold,
and thus everything is illogical.
In this matter too, other disputants
desire liberation of the <s>Puruṣa</s>,
and, in accordance with reason, regard <s>Prakṛti</s>
as indeed <s>karma-prakṛti</s> (nature constituted by action).
And since she is of manifold forms,
and is connected with transformability,
and serves as the bondage of the <s>Ātman</s>,
the faults mentioned above do not arise.
The incorporeal does not become corporeal,
nor does the corporeal become incorporeal;
therefore, by bondage and by reasoning,
the connection of the <s>Ātman</s> with it is untenable.
The objection that through the experience of touch and so forth of the body,
it does not so occur, is an overstatement;
for this connection is born of mutual pervading,
and thus bondage and the like are tenable.
The connection of the <s>Ātman</s> with the corporeal
is possible, as with space (<s>ākāśa</s>);
and the occurrence of harm and the like
is like that of knowledge through liquor and such.
Thus the doctrine of <s>Prakṛti</s> too
should be understood as indeed true,
and because it was stated by <s>Kapila</s>,
for he was a divine great sage.
Fourth Cluster.
(1) Introduction to the Refutation of the Doctrine of <s>Kṣaṇikavāda</s> (Momentariness).
Others consider the entire world
to be bound by afflictions and <s>karma</s>,
perishing every moment — the greatly wise ones;
and yet others hold it to be mere cognition (<s>jñānamātra</s>).
They say: "Everything is momentary,
because there is no connection with a cause of destruction;
because of the capacity for causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyāsamarthatva</s>),
because of transformation, and because destruction is observed."
"And since in the world only cognition (<s>jñāna</s>)
is experienced as cognition,
no object exists apart from it;
therefore that [external object] does not exist."
To this too, others respond:
"Since memory and the like would be impossible,
and since external objects are experienced,
all this is groundless."
Since memory pertains to previously experienced objects,
and since worldly memory
pertains to a different time — in what is thus impermanent,
this primary sense does not hold.
"That disciple is this teacher" —
recognition does not hold;
curiosity about what is seen, agitation,
activity, and attainment —
the enjoyment of what one has done oneself
would be entirely precluded;
that which is the cause for the practice of moral conduct
would perish at the very moment it arises.
"In our view, all conventional usage
is held with reference to the continuum (<s>saṃtāna</s>);
and since that is one and the same,
why should it not be justified?
In whatever continuum
the impression of <s>karma</s> is deposited,
the fruit is produced in that very continuum,
like the redness in cotton."
This too is mere assertion,
not established by the relation of cause and effect;
the continuum is different, and this is unjustified
for those who hold the doctrine of <s>asatkārya</s> (non-pre-existence of the effect).

children.text: (2) bhāva abhāva bana jātā hai isa mata kā khaṃḍana
children.translated_text: (2) Refutation of the view that being arises from non-being.
Non-being does not become being,
as in the case of a hare's horn;
and being does not become non-being here,
due to the faults of its arising and the like.
If being becomes non-being, then its arising
and then its destruction would follow;
that which is destroyed would again come into being,
and there would always be destruction, never stability.
If it is of the nature of lasting only a moment,
then lasting for a second moment and beyond
is also justified for it,
and thus the statement made is not transgressed.
If it does not last even for a moment,
its non-lasting is logically untenable;
and "it does not last afterward either" — thus
the non-existence of what exists is established.

children.text: na tad bhavati cet kiṃ na
children.translated_text: If it does not exist — why not?
It is always existent, precisely because
its not-being is exactly its being —
so the wise ones understand.
Since what is to be produced
is occasional, that is certain;
"it does not exist because it is void" — but how can
what is not void not exist, since it is not void?
This is equal to its arising;
its cessation — does it not belong to it?
Let being not exist due to voidness —
but how can non-being be being, and being-non-being?
Since it is born only from its own cause,
and is of its own nature,
and since it immediately follows —
the same applies in the other case too.
Its arising is not without a cause;
in what is void, its own nature does not exist;
therefore, how can that come into being?
How is this consistent by reasoning?
That very being is the cause of that;
that is established by its very remaining as such;
its own cessation is its inherent nature —
is it not like that of being itself?
Inherent nature, like knowability,
is not such that it would be unjustified for it;
in the absence of that, there would be no knowledge of it —
how then the course of its cessation?
Since what is of such inherent nature
is indeed grasped as such
by direct perception, its course is thereby established;
this is nowhere uncertain.
"That is a superimposition" — if one says "it is not" —
then it is grasped in its reality;
from grasping its real nature,
due to infinite regress, that too would be unreal.
All is grasped by this;
but certainty is determined again
by the superimposition of limited grasping —
thus the establishment of reality.
Certainty in one case, in another,
even from the experience of partless entities,
does not hold likewise, due to the absence of keenness.
This is an unprecedented darkness.
For beyond the momentary nature of its own being,
there is emptiness (<s>tucchatā</s>) due to its cessation.
That [emptiness] is not grasped by a single moment—
this is properly understood from [valid] cognition.
And when that [emptiness] is not grasped,
the determination that 'it is thus' [cannot arise].
For the sense organ is not accepted by the wise
as apprehending what is past and so forth.
Even at the end, there is no perception of it,
since [what remains are] potsherds and the like.
That [collection of potsherds] is not the absence of a pot
cognized as a positive entity.
The cognition of that [absence] does not arise from the cognition of those [potsherds],
due to the distinction between obstruction [and its absence].
But if that very [entity] were to become non-existent,
there would be continuity due to the non-interruption of [positive] entities.
Therefore it must necessarily be accepted
that beyond that, it is simply empty (<s>tuccham</s>).
What is knowable as existent is indeed known—
this is reasonable even by another [line of argument].
There is no identity between those two [existence and non-existence] through origination and the like,
due to the distinction between the empty and the non-empty.
This should be understood also from the difference of cessation
and from the difference of cognition.
By this, the following is refuted—
what was stated by one who fancies himself a logician:
'Nothing whatsoever exists there;
it simply does not exist at all.'
For this alternative would apply only to a [positive] entity,
since a positive rule conforms to a real thing.
'A [positive] entity does not come into being'—this was stated;
but also 'a non-entity comes into being' [is implied].
By this, even regarding the thesis of causelessness,
since [it involves] coming into being after not having been, [which implies] a nature of destruction,
the implication of the fault of destroying existence
has been refuted.
And what was rejected—[namely] that the charge
of existence being indestructible has not been warded off—
[we reply:] the non-existence at that time has the form of emptiness,
and is declared indestructible due to the non-attainment of [positive] being.
That which is the non-becoming of a [positive] entity,
and that which is the becoming of a non-entity—
the alternative stated regarding that which has such a property
is not contradictory.
'That itself does not come into being'—this
appears as if contradictory,
but [it is so] precisely because of the contact with a real thing
and the negation of [its] becoming.
Since the non-existence of an existent
is in no way tenable,
'a [positive] entity does not become a non-entity'—
this is thereby established.
(3) Refutation of the view that non-existence becomes existence
Section: Refutation of this doctrine
But if the existent-ness of the non-existent is conjoined,
then due to the conjunction of that kind of capacity,
there is no non-existence [of it], yet in the absence of that [capacity],
there is no existence of that, just as with something else.
The non-existent arises—indeed
that for which there exists a cause
possessing a distinctive capacity—
hence the establishment of the existence of that [effect].
When everything is absolutely non-existent,
the possession of a distinctive capacity
by the cause is not logically [tenable],
for what is merely imagined does not shine forth [as real].
That does not establish the existence of that [effect],

children.text: tad eva hi tadā na yat
children.translated_text: for that which at that time is not that very [thing]—
therefore, let those who wish this [understand]:
it does not [follow] for that, due to logical impossibility.
By the nature of things, that which
comes into being immediately after that—
nothing else follows from that; and here by name alone
there is no such purpose [served].
Even without a name, by its true nature,
without a distinctive positive injunction—
let it be considered: if by proper reasoning
[it is established] by the nature of things, then it is indeed so.
But if everything has the capacity to produce [everything],
then the arising of [any] entity from that would follow.
Even taking recourse to causation,
there is no existence of that [effect], just as with something else.
Moreover, that cause does not exist
at the time of the coming into being of the effect.
Therefore it is not the producer of that [effect],
since it is non-existent at that time, just as what is remote.
And the immediate [subsequent] existence of that
is purposeless, since it follows from the nature of things alone.
And the destruction and origination
of cause and effect are simultaneous.
Are those two [destruction and origination] different or non-different?
If different, how could there be a distinction between those two?
But if destruction and origination are non-different,
then they would be simultaneous.
And the cause-effect relationship
is not tenable when that [simultaneity] obtains,
since both are devoid of
the state of being grounded in each other.
If this property-property-bearer relationship
is imagined as having [positive] existence,
then the cause-effect relationship would not hold,
since that [relationship] is entirely absent.
The property-bearer is not imagined; rather, the property-
property-bearer relationship is imagined.
The former is the cause, being partless;
the latter is called the effect.
Since the prior [moment] itself has the nature of non-existence
when [it undergoes] becoming, alas, whence the subsequent?
But if that very [prior moment] has the nature of non-existence,
then existence from the non-existent [follows]—hence it is not valid.
'Dependent on that, the origination of that'—
this statement is empty (<s>tuccham</s>).
And [this is so] due to overextension (<s>atiprasaṅga</s>)—
thus says the great sage.
That which is not in all respects of such a nature
without [having] the nature of a real thing,
[and] the effect [arising] immediately after the cause—
it quickly [falls] from the sky; therefore it is not that.
Even the supposition of attributing
to that the nature of that very thing is enough [to show the flaw].
It is not logically sound, due to deficiency of reasoning—
[it is] like the affliction of birth by <s>Rāhu</s>.
Since the determination [of causation is based] merely
on the state of arising immediately after that,
everything would be the effect of everything,
since there is no distinction in that state of being.
Since [conditions such as] being in the same location, etc.
are unestablished, and since there is no invariable concomitance,
and since all [candidates] are undifferentiated,
there is no ground for the restriction [of specific causation].
Even the arising of one thing from another
that is seen at another time in the [causal] continuum—
that very same [arising] from something situated in another location—
even that does not serve as an invalidation.
By this, the following is refuted—
what was stated by the subtle-minded one:
'The non-existent has no capacity to produce entities;
a different state of that is not that [original entity].'
The existence of something that invariably [arises]
immediately after a [particular] entity—
that is regarded as its effect; that very [existence]
is the origination of an entity, having that as its nature.
The origination of the non-existent is also declared
with respect to this, due to [its] prior non-existence.
Not through the conjunction of existence with the non-existent,
but from the cause in the form of [producing] the effect.
And that [objection] has been refuted: without the cause
attaining the status of effect,
the non-existent has the capacity to produce entities,
and a different state of that is indeed that [entity].
The existence immediately after an entity
would occur without such-ness of that [causal relation].
From the conjunction of existence with the non-existent [falling] from the sky—
thus it is not the effect of that.
The origination of the non-existent is also
not [established] from the prior non-existence of this alone.

children.text: kiṃ tv asat sad bhavaty evam
children.translated_text: Rather, whether the non-existent becomes existent—
let this be properly investigated.
And this, as stated [before], by reasoning
is in no way tenable, since
non-existence does not attain the state of existence—
this is established from that.
(4) Impossibility of the totality-causation doctrine (<s>sāmagrīkāraṇatāvāda</s>) within momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikavāda</s>)
Even the totality (<s>sāmagrī</s>) of form and the like,
arising from distinctive conditions,
that is imagined as the producer
of cognition and the like—that too is purposeless.
If the capacity to produce cognition
is accepted for all [components equally]—
form and the like—then the differentiation of effects
from those [components] is not tenable.
Multiple effects such as form, light, etc.
arise from those [components],
and [they arise] from exactly that many [causes]—
let it be considered how this [can be explained].
And the supposition of the capacity of many [causes]
in producing a single [effect] is not valid,
since the multiplicity of those [causes]
contradicts the unity of that [effect].
How could a single [effect] arise here
dependent on all of those [causes] without remainder?
That which is one has a single nature—
but that cannot arise from multiple [causes].
Since when those [causes] have different natures,
there is multiplicity among them,
and given that [the effect] is produced by those [collectively],
how could it have a unitary form?
What arises dependent on a single capacity
does not [arise] from another,
since that would entail non-difference between the two;
and if [the capacities are] different, there is difference between those two as well.
Nothing whatsoever arises
dependent on a single [combined] capacity.
If [you say] that is because it has the nature
of [being produced by] the capacity of all—that is not so.
If that [effect] has the nature of each individual [capacity],
then the nature described [above] would be appropriate.
But that collective capacity of all
is not devoid of the individual [capacities].
And here it has been stated: 'the supposition
that these have the nature of that
is not valid,' due to overextension and other [faults],
since alternative explanations are possible.
If the capacity of form and the like
is also posited with respect to other [effects],

children.text: na tad eva tad ity evaṃ
children.translated_text: then 'that is not that very thing'—thus
how can diverse [capacities operate] in a single [effect]?
Even from the standpoint of the totality,
the differentiation of effects is proclaimed thus.
Since a single [totality] produces diverse effects,
even that [differentiation] is undermined.
And the combination [of causes] in the form of
material cause and the like for a single [effect] is not coherent
when examined with reasoning here—
the supposition of its [being a single] unity [fails].
Form, by whatever nature
is the material cause (<s>upādānakāraṇa</s>) of [another] form,
becomes the efficient cause (<s>nimittakāraṇa</s>) of cognition—
does it do so by that same [nature] or by another?
If by that very same [nature], then cognition
having the nature of awareness is not tenable.
If by another, then form would by necessity
have two natures—an absurd consequence.
If [you say] the moment of form is the establisher of cognition
through the exclusion of [what is] not a producer of cognition—
[we ask:] since it is not cognition [itself],
how is it the establisher of form?
For that [moment], through the differentiation of exclusion,
is said to produce form and the like—
this is stated for practical purposes,
though in reality it has a single nature.
Why is this [moment] not said to produce odor
through the exclusion of not producing odor?
If [you say] because that [exclusion] does not exist,
then the existence of the other [exclusion] would [also] follow as absurd.
Thus, even given the differentiation of exclusions,
the multiple-nature of that [moment]
necessarily follows—and that
is vitiated by the acceptance of what is unreasonable.
The eye and other [sense organs] have natures
that produce distinct effects.
If there is differentiation also in cognition, [well and good];
if not, then differentiation is not tenable.
Thus, even from the standpoint of the totality,
in every way [this doctrine] is untenable.
Whatever [is claimed about] the cause-effect relationship—
that too is mere assertion.
(5) Impossibility of the impressed-impressioner relationship (<s>vāsyavāsakabhāva</s>) in the doctrine of momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikavāda</s>)
Since diversity is not sublated here,
how can there be experience of what is self-created?
Even when this [diversity] exists, let it be considered
that [experience is impossible] due to the absolute difference between those [moments].
If [you claim it is possible] due to the relationship of impressed and impressioner (<s>vāsyavāsakabhāva</s>)—
that is not [valid], since even that is impossible.
How is it impossible?
Due to the untenable nature of [every possible] alternative.
Is the impression (<s>vāsanā</s>) different
from the impressioner or non-different?
If different, the impressioner itself is devoid of it,
and it does not impress another [moment] at all.
If non-different, then there is no transference
of it, just as with the form of the impressioner [itself].
And if transference [to] the impressed were established,
the establishment of a permanent substance-part would result.
If [you say] even without transference
it does impress—
then there would be overextension (<s>atiprasaṅga</s>),
and that is excluded from valid reasoning.
And the impressed-impressioner relationship
is not, in reality, other than
the cause-effect relationship—this is the logical [conclusion];
and that [cause-effect relationship] has been shown to be untenable.

children.text: (6) kṣaṇikavāda meṃ kāryakāraṇa jñāna kī anupapatti
children.translated_text: (6) Impossibility of causal cognition in the doctrine of momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikavāda</s>)
That [cause] has the nature of producing that [effect],
and the other [effect] has the nature of being produced—
hence, due to the fixed restriction of natures,
that [relationship] is never unreasonable.
In the absence of apprehension of both,
the supposition of such a relation
is not proper; and by a single [cognition]
the apprehension of both is not possible for you.
Just as two cognitions do not
cognize a single object,
so too a single cognition does not
cognize two objects.
By the nature of things, regarding the true nature of those two,
even with a single [cognition] there is such apprehension—
this is no invalidation. But a single [cognition] does not
apprehend two [objects]—this [has been established].
The apprehension of those two as such
never consists in the apprehension of the other.
Since it is never tenable,
how then is it not an invalidation?
And if [there is] such apprehension [of causation] everywhere,
without the apprehension of invariable absence [of the effect when the cause is absent],
how could the cognition of fire etc.
follow merely from the apprehension of smoke etc.?
The absence of the immediately preceding [moment]
in that [case] is untenable,
since even when both [conditions] are equal,
alas, [the effect] is sometimes not observed.
There is no equality between those two, since for one
there is a cause of the cause.
By convention, [the cognition] pertains to the object of that cause,
but this is not so for the other.
That [cognition] which grasps fire alone
and which is the cause of the cause of [inferential] cognition—
even that [operates] thus; and from the cause of that,
there is also the cognition of that [fire] from that [smoke-]cognition.
That cognition [of fire] which is not
the immediately preceding [cause] of the cognition of smoke—
since it was not of such a nature—therefore here
there is no cognition of that [fire] from that [smoke-]cognition either.
Alas, what is the meaning of 'of such a nature'?
If [it means] from the state of being thus [i.e., causally related]—
then in the other case, let it be understood that
only one cognition grasps that [object].
In the absence of that, the otherwise-ness
of that [cognition] is also found in this [case].
What is immediately past and what is long past—
those are in reality equivalent.
By this, [the claim that] the cognition of smoke
is by nature born from the cognition of fire,
and that this is what produces the conceptual construction, and nothing else—
let this be accepted as refuted.
Therefore, since in some manner or other, by a single [cognition],
there is no apprehension of those two [cause and effect],
from the absence of such cognition, the supposition
of such a [causal] relation is not proper.
How then is [causation] established
by perception and non-apprehension (<s>anupalambha</s>)?
Therefore, causality
is not ascertained, due to the uncertainty of such existence and the like.
The prior [moment] and the subsequent one here—
since the other is certainly not apprehended [along with the one]—
are [each] grasped [separately]; hence this [cognition] is not from that,
but [this is] not a perception of what is beyond the senses.
Conceptual construction also, by this reasoning,
is not tenable, for it is not of such a kind,
since it is born from the impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>) of that,
and due to the momentariness of everything.
This is not so—in the absence of continuity of awareness,
the determination of that does not hold good.
Taking a neutral standpoint,
let this be considered by oneself.
The cognition of fire etc. here
does not attain the status of being smoke-cognition,
since [they differ] in form (<s>ākāra</s>)—
whence then the continuity of awareness?
Due to the abandonment of that form
and the establishment of another form—
The continuity of cognition, which is the instigator of a prolonged single
determinate cognition,
Since it is established by <s>svasaṃvedana</s> (self-awareness),
the supposition that this is erroneous
is not justified by reasoning,
because it would lead to the absurd consequence that all cognition is erroneous.
Through prolonged determinate cognition,
the ascertainment of perishability and so forth arises;
and if this were erroneous,
the assertion that it is so would not be reasonable.
Therefore, it must necessarily be accepted
that even some conceptual cognition
is, in some way or another,
entirely non-erroneous in nature.
This being so, our position stands
by virtue of the reasoning already stated:
the continuity of cognition, because of the impossibility of the production of parts,
and because of the consequence of over-extension.
From objects of a different kind,
this cognition itself, though of a different kind,
since it is accepted as such, therefore from this
there arises an undoubted ascertainment regarding that.
When there is the state of being produced by that particular thing,
the connection with its existence is certain;
for its existence is nothing other than that,
and the production from the product is likewise.
Even when there is the state of being a product of that,
this should be considered by the wise:
since the existence is indeed from that alone,
and that depends upon another.
Thus the implication of continuity
arises from the meaning of the words themselves;
and any alternative interpretation of this
is entirely contradicted by reasoning.
That effect which is devoid of the capacity for that form,
is like any other effect;
there is no operation of that either,
nor is there any expectation anywhere, due to the absence of reality.
Nevertheless, the supposition that those two alone
have that nature
is, because of its equality with other cases,
merely an indication of blind bias.

children.text: (7) buddhavacanoṃ kī sahāyatā se kṣaṇikavāda kā khaṃḍana
children.translated_text: (7) buddhavacanoṃ kī sahāyatā se kṣaṇikavāda kā khaṃḍana
Moreover, if momentariness is accepted,
even the authoritative meaning is contradicted;
and the bringing about of this contradiction
is not the result of a small amount of ignorance.
"Ninety-one <s>kalpas</s> (aeons) ago,
a man was slain by me with a weapon;
by that ripening of <s>karma</s>,
I have been wounded in the foot, O <s>bhikṣus</s> (monks)."
"Me" and "by me" — this self-reference,
and the act of killing attributed to that self —
since this was stated by one who is himself an <s>āpta</s> (authority),
what is this insistence on momentariness?
If it be said that this was stated by the <s>Bhagavān</s> (Blessed One)
with reference to the <s>santāna</s> (continuum),
then the causal-resultant relationship
is not compatible with the expression "to me."
If it be said that "mine" means by the power of the cause,
and that this is the intended meaning,
there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid cognition) here, since that intended meaning
is considered to be beyond perception.
If the teaching of that is the <s>pramāṇa</s>,
then it cannot have a different meaning;
and if you ask what is the <s>pramāṇa</s> for that too,
it is this same authoritative statement mentioned before.
Likewise, there is another such instance: "The earth
endures for a <s>kalpa</s> (aeon)" — this was stated
by the <s>Bhagavān</s> (Blessed One) himself,
addressing the <s>bhikṣus</s> (monks) directly.
"The five external [sense objects] are cognized by two [cognitions]" —
this and other authoritative statements too
should be understood as <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid authority),
as they establish the matter under discussion.
Because, if momentariness holds for these,
there would be no cognition by two;
for when they are grasped at different times by these two,
the meaning of those words would be established.
But if grasped at the same time,
then one of the two would be invalid as a <s>pramāṇa</s>;
because it would be grasping what is already grasped,
and thus the word of the <s>Tathāgata</s> would be false.
When form and the like are discerned by a sense organ,
immediately thereafter,
with respect to that same form and the like,
mental cognition arises.
Thus there is no contradiction,
since the state of being cognized by two exists.
But if this applies to all five by the same reasoning,
then this too is inconsistent.
For not even one is cognized by two,
since each is cognized by only one;
if this is said with reference to the universal,
that is not so, because of the absurd consequence that universals would be real.
Even if they were real, sensory cognition
is certainly not considered to have that as its object;
thus the state of being cognized by two
does not truly hold when moments are different.
All the proofs of momentariness
have been refuted by this;
nevertheless, hereafter some further points
will be stated specifically regarding that topic.
pāṃcavāṃ stabaka
(1)bāhyārthakhaṃḍana khaṃḍana
The doctrine of <s>vijñānamātra</s> (consciousness-only) also
is not properly established.
For no <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid cognition) whatsoever
exists in reality in the absence of objects.
There is no perception, because in the absence
of an object-support, it is not accepted as such;
nor is there inference, because of the impossibility
of a valid logical mark of that nature.
An object that has fulfilled the conditions of perceptibility
yet is not perceived —
from that, by non-apprehension alone,
its absence is ascertained.
The fulfillment of the conditions of perceptibility
consists in the combination of the other causal factors;
and if these are of that very nature,
how could its non-establishment be the case?
If it be said that they are of such a nature as to produce
together with the object,
then when the object exists, they would indeed produce;
otherwise they would not be of that nature.
If the supposition of their being of that nature
is made with reference to their capacity,
well then, that is established for you
from occasional perception.
Otherwise, how is their capacity
established by reasoning?
For in the world, the capacity for cooking and the like
is not established for a horse and similar things.
If it be said that this is stated
from another's perspective, then the objection is that
the object that has fulfilled the conditions of perceptibility
is perceived by that person.
And even if it is not grasped
due to the absence of means of grasping it,
its non-existence does not follow
merely from that, because of the absurd consequence of over-extension.
Consciousness is self-cognized,
but the object is not, due to the absence of valid reasoning;
therefore, in the cognition of that,
the grasping of it is not established.
And thus, from the very non-grasping,
its absence is ascertained;
therefore, what is the use of saying that no <s>pramāṇa</s>
exists in the absence of objects?
That which has the form of grasping an object
is accepted as self-cognized;
in the cognition of that, there is grasping of it —
then what is it that is not established?
"This is cognition of a pot" and so on — from <s>saṃvitti</s> (self-awareness),
from its activity in that regard,
from the attainment of purposeful action,
from memory, and from the nature of curious interest.
But if consciousness is mere cognition,
then consciousness would be just cognition and nothing more;
activity and the like would then not arise,
which is well-known in both common experience and scripture.
And if consciousness grasps something other than that,
then its aversion toward the object is groundless;
and with respect to another cognition too, the same applies —
the non-cognition of that and so forth.
And the impossibility of reasoning regarding the object
that is proclaimed from the standpoint of the doctrine of universals —
through the door of apprehended and the like,
that same objection applies equally to the doctrine of consciousness.
That which is not exclusively apprehended,
due to the absence of an apprehender on earth,
and that which is exclusively an apprehender
is untenable due to the absence of the apprehended.
Due to contradiction, it cannot have both forms;
otherwise it would be non-existent;
being devoid of intrinsic nature,
how can its existence be justified?
For consciousness is considered in reality
to have illumination as its sole intrinsic nature;
and being intransitive,
it illuminates by itself alone.
Just as in expressions like "he sits," "he lies down," and so on,
he himself acts without an object —
so it is said in this world;
let consciousness be accepted likewise.
It is said: let this be considered
by oneself right now —
whether, in the absence of a <s>pramāṇa</s>,
this is properly established.
Thus, if it cannot even illuminate
its own self,
then this position is not tenable;
otherwise there would be no stable determination.
And if there is stable determination of reality,
then that which illuminates the nature of things
is certain; therefore, how could
its intransitivity be the case?
That which establishes this
is in fact erroneous in reality;
and if you say "it is non-erroneous in that respect,"
there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> for that either.
A non-erroneous determination from an erroneous cognition
is not justified by reasoning.
If it be said that this is observed in the case of those with eye-disease
and the like regarding the sense organs — that is not so.
The cognition of defects in sense organs and the like
is not erroneous in the way that other errors are;
if that cognition were erroneous in that regard,
the erroneous would become non-erroneous.
And mere illumination
is never intransitive in the world;
this is not properly established even in the case of a lamp and the like,
and therefore this argument is pointless.
Proof from a mere example
that is entirely dissimilar to the subject
does not establish the thesis;
that too is mere words.
(2) vijñānādvaitavāda meṃ mokṣa kī anupapatti
Furthermore, if consciousness-only is accepted,
there is no distinction whatsoever
between <s>saṃsāra</s> (cyclic existence) and <s>apavarga</s> (liberation);
and thus this doctrine is proclaimed in vain.
For <s>citta</s> (mind) itself is <s>saṃsāra</s>,
when pervaded by <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) such as <s>rāga</s> (attachment) and the like;
that very same, when freed from them,
is called the end of existence.
Since the group of <s>kleśas</s> such as <s>rāga</s> and the like
is not considered different from consciousness,
and when that has exclusively one nature,
what is pervaded by what?
It is consciousness itself that is afflicted;
if its afflicted nature is due to that,
then like blue and the like, that entity
would be established as being just like that forever.
And in liberation, its existence through differentiation
would be like the purification of a cloth;
from that, the establishment of external objects
would follow — which is undesirable to you.
If it be said that it is of such a nature by its very essence,
and that itself is its afflicted state,
then since it is neither less nor more than that,
by what means could liberation be conceived?
If it be said that even in the absence of external objects,
there is an error characterized by the duality of apprehended and apprehender,
like the illusion of seeing two moons,
and this is our afflicted state —
let this be so; however, the cause of that
would arise from a different cause;
this would be like the absence of the eye-disease —
without it, there is no seeing of two moons.
And the cause of that is not non-existent,
nor is it mere cognition;
for then affliction would always persist,
and thus liberation would not be possible.
And in the absence of liberation,
all deliberation would be pointless;
and even if it always exists,
let this be properly considered.
Since the doctrine of <s>vijñānamātra</s> (consciousness-only)
is not established by reasoning in this way,
the attachment of the wise
to this doctrine is therefore not justified.
chaṭhā stabaka

children.text: (1) nirhetuka vināśa se kṣaṇikavāda kī siddhi nahīṃ
children.translated_text: (1) nirhetuka vināśa se kṣaṇikavāda kī siddhi nahīṃ
What was stated earlier in this very text
as proof of momentariness —
the absence of a cause of destruction and so forth —
that is now examined.
Whether an entity is perishable
due to a cause or without a cause — when this is considered,
the claim of the absence of a cause of destruction
is not reasonable.
That it is perishable depending on a cause
is accepted in the same way
as, for you, a cause
is the producer of a specific effect.
Just so, that entity arises
from its own cause alone, being of that very nature,
and upon encountering an auxiliary cause,
produces a specific effect.
Nothing further is done
by that auxiliary cause to this entity,
since they exist simultaneously —
and thus this has been stated by you yourself.
That which is considered a helper, an opponent,
or an auxiliary cause —
all of these are with reference to the continuum,
never at a single moment.
Even though there is no differentiation in the cause
produced by the auxiliary,
there is differentiation in the effect,
due to the attainment of a superadded excellence produced by that.
And if the cause is not of that nature,
then that differentiation of the effect is also not justified,
because of the attainment of birth in a homogeneous moment,
just like something of a different kind.
And it is misplaced partiality
that posits, regarding the cause, an expectation
that does not help it;
this effect-attribution is stated in vain.
Because for that too, the same applies —
being the producer of a specific effect,
relying on the cause of existence —
this has been demonstrated by reasoning.
And thus, the consideration of something separate and the like
is entirely useless here,
which is carried out by the wise
with reference to destruction based on what is to be destroyed.
Moreover, if destruction is causeless,
the state of being a killer is not justified,
since no one at any time
is ever destroyed by anyone anywhere.
If he is a killer because he is the cause
of the arising of a particular continuum —
that is not so, because the origination of a continuum
is impossible.
Since destruction and origination of a continuum
are conventional, like a sky-flower,
they do not exist; and since it is not a property of that,
how can there be a cause for its arising?
If the producer of a dissimilar moment
is said to be the killer — that is not so,
because that would also arise of its own accord,
and there would be no distinction in the status of producer.
If a killer is postulated on the basis of
the affliction of thinking "I will kill this one" —
this is not possible, since according to your own principles,
this very thing is not justified.
The affliction, being the production of a quality,
does not arise from the unafflicted alone;
nor even from that which has an associate of another kind,
because of the absence of any superadded excellence in that.
If it be said that by attaining that, it becomes of that nature,
and therefore that is so —
then even in the position of destruction having a cause,
there is no objection, since one attains the cause of destruction.
Others, however, relying on the produced entity,
with reference to its own nature and the like,
state thus: the causelessness
of the producer in every respect.
That which has its own nature does not produce,
because of the absurd consequence that it would be futile;
and due to the fault of impossibility of production and the like,
even the other is not justified.
And the existence of both and the like
is not possible due to contradiction and impossibility;
others hold that it is due to the existence of its own cessation and the like,
and due to the absence of the effect.
And there is no contradiction with perception
regarding the status of being a producer,
because of the non-establishment of that by the reasoning
that prohibits conventional usage.
