In the absence of a <s>pramāṇa</s>,
even the opponent's conventional usage is prohibited.
The subject matter of valid cognition and language,
likewise, should be examined here too.

children.text: (2) arthakriyākāritva se kṣaṇikavāda kī siddhi nahīṃ
children.translated_text: (2) The doctrine of momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikavāda</s>) is not established through causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyākāritva</s>)
The capacity for causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyāsamarthatva</s>)
that is proclaimed in the momentary (<s>kṣaṇika</s>),
since destruction occurs immediately after origination,
should be understood as logically untenable.
Either that causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyā</s>) is itself,
or it is something other — there are only two possibilities.
If identical, there is no capacity for it,
since it would arise from something other than itself.
It cannot sustain itself, by logical reasoning,
since destruction follows immediately upon birth.
Nor can it bring about destruction, by valid reasoning,
since destruction would arise from its own cause.
If different, that something other has the capacity
in something else — this is not coherent.
Therefore, this amounts to the existence of something other,
and that is not logically justified without evidence.
Since the non-existent cannot be born as existent,
even when something else exists and persists,
if that very thing were to become such,
then surely the continuity (<s>anvaya</s>) remains unestablished — how?
What they call 'existence' (<s>bhūti</s>) as action (<s>kriyā</s>),
that too is not tenable anywhere,
due to contradiction with the nature of being
both agent (<s>kartṛ</s>) and experiencer (<s>bhoktṛ</s>) — let this be considered.
And it has been shown that what is past
has no capacity for that action.
Nor is there any other ordinary
meaning of words here — this is logically untenable.

children.text: (3) rūparūpāntaraṇa se kṣaṇikavāda kī siddhi nahīṃ
children.translated_text: (3) The doctrine of momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikavāda</s>) is not established through transformation into another form
Transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>) also is not a valid reason
for establishing momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikatva</s>),
since even when there is constant change,
the perception of that very nature persists.
Because there is no transition to something entirely different,
nor is there absolutely no change at all —
<s>pariṇāma</s> (transformation) is established by valid cognition
and is indeed accepted by the learned.
And as for what is said: 'We declare
impermanence as non-constancy of state' —
this does not become something entirely different,
therefore, given otherness, continuity (<s>anvaya</s>) is certain.
'This very thing does not remain this,'
and 'that does not become this' —
alas, this is contradictory, and moreover, something different
would then have a beginning, which is an undesired consequence.
The destruction of milk is indeed curd,
as is observed — being connected with dairy essence.
But it does not become oil, etc., hence it is established that
<s>pariṇāma</s> (transformation) entails continuity (<s>anvaya</s>).
The non-existent can never become existent,
and the existent is never absolutely non-existent,
due to the absence of capacity, over-extension,
and the loss of the nature of being existent.
Therefore, by reasoning about the permanent and impermanent,
that thing is such because of its being so,
accompanied by cognition, it is correctly
understood through transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>).

children.text: (4)antatogāmī nāśa se kṣaṇikavāda kī siddhi nahīṃ
children.translated_text: (4) The doctrine of momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikavāda</s>) is not established through ultimate destruction
The observation of decay at the end,
as proof of decay at every moment,
since that itself has the nature of such,
is never logically tenable.
If it had the nature of decay from the beginning,
how could it be observed only at the end?
Due to the deception of successive similar productions
as previously stated.
From the observation of decay at the end,
decay unseen at the beginning is inferred.
Because it is obscured by the similar,
the non-apprehension of that is due to the apprehension of that [similar thing].
This too is untenable, for
what is similar is indeed different.
When the difference is not apprehended, how can there be
apprehension of it as having that nature?
If one says that cognition is determined by that object,
and it does not apprehend the difference due to non-apprehension of other things,
then this is equally applicable —
how can there be any progress through another?
And in the absence of such progress,
this statement is surely empty:
'Because it is obscured by the similar,
the non-apprehension of that is due to the apprehension of that.'
And if this is accepted, then necessarily
a single cognition that apprehends many things,
a continuous (<s>anvayin</s>) cognition must be admitted —
how then can everything be momentary (<s>kṣaṇika</s>)?
And an object is apprehended by cognition,
but not in the perception of another.
In the absence of that, since that [cognition] exists,
at some point, in reality,
even when there is apprehension, when cognition
perishes immediately after arising,
then how does it know
the momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikatva</s>) of that object?
Since that itself has that nature,
since it arises from its own self —
just as blue and so forth have such form —
this does not hold, due to the doubt of falsity.
Nor even through one's own inference,
since there is the possibility of difference in properties,
and since the inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>) transgresses the property,
and due to the inapplicability of having that nature, etc.
That the permanent (<s>nitya</s>) is incapable of causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyā</s>) —
this too cannot be established by such reasoning,
since all cognition (<s>vijñāna</s>) without exception
would then be momentary (<s>kṣaṇika</s>).
Likewise, since objects have a variegated nature,
it is not that causal efficacy is impossible for them.
Surely causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyā</s>), by reasoning,
manifests both sequentially and simultaneously.

children.text: (5) kṣaṇikavāda tathā vijñānavāda ke pratipādana kā eka saṃbhava āśayaviśeṣa
children.translated_text: (5) A possible special intent behind the teaching of <s>kṣaṇikavāda</s> (momentariness doctrine) and <s>vijñānavāda</s> (consciousness-only doctrine)
Others, however, declare thus,
in order to remove this fixation:
'Everything is momentary (<s>kṣaṇika</s>)' —
this was said by the <s>Buddha</s> not as ultimate truth,
and 'consciousness-only' (<s>vijñānamātra</s>) likewise
was said to remove attachment to externals,
depending on certain disciples (<s>vineya</s>),
or because it was fitting to teach thus.
And this too is not unreasonable,
for the <s>Buddha</s>, the great sage (<s>Mahāmuni</s>),
like a skilled physician, without necessity,
does not prescribe what is ultimately false (<s>dravyāsatya</s>).
(6) Refutation of <s>śūnyavāda</s> (the doctrine of emptiness)
But other discerning ones declare
that everything is empty (<s>śūnya</s>).
Neither permanent nor impermanent —
no entity is established through reasoning.
The permanent is untenable due to absence of causal efficacy,
and due to the contradiction between sequential and simultaneous.
The impermanent also, due to the absence of
origination and decay, is never tenable.
And the cognitions of origination and decay
are like causes of delight for the deluded —
like a maiden's dream, they should be understood
as being like the cognition of giving birth to a son, etc.
To this too, others respond:
Is there any means of valid cognition (<s>pramāṇa</s>)
for establishing reality in this manner,
or is it too simply empty?
If it is empty, then reality is well-established [as non-empty];
if it exists, how can there be emptiness?
For that very thing would exist —
let this be properly considered.
Even without a means of valid cognition,
reality might be established thus —
otherwise not — it is quite clear that
this is mere divine play (<s>Īśvara</s>-like arbitrariness).
If, setting aside the stated means of knowledge,
this entity is said to be empty,
then, the object to be established being empty,
surely the effort is in vain.
And if that too is non-empty,
then, due to the multiplicity of questioners,
the undesired consequence of abundant non-emptiness
would follow.
For as many as there are valid cognitions,
and whatever objects are to be established thereby,
all of those exist —
hence the non-emptiness of many things.
Thus, the doctrine of emptiness (<s>śūnyavāda</s>) too
was stated in accordance with those disciples (<s>vineya</s>) to be trained,
with a special intent (<s>abhiprāya</s>) — so it is said,
as observed by the knower of reality.
Seventh Chapter (<s>Saptama Stabaka</s>)
(1) Defense of the Jain doctrine of permanence-cum-impermanence (<s>nityānityatvavāda</s>)
Others, however, say: the world, which is beginningless,
consists of the conscious (<s>jīva</s>) and the non-conscious (<s>ajīva</s>),
and is endowed with origination (<s>utpāda</s>), decay (<s>vyaya</s>), and permanence (<s>dhrauvya</s>) —
so say those who have labored over the scriptures (<s>śāstra</s>).
One who desires gold in the form of a pot or a crown,
in the events of destruction, origination, and persistence,
experiences grief, joy, and equanimity respectively —
people do so with good reason.
One who vows to drink milk does not consume curd;
one who vows to consume curd does not drink milk;
one who vows against dairy consumes neither —
therefore, reality (<s>tattva</s>) has a threefold nature.
To this too, others object:
The three are mutually contradictory;
that all three could exist in one and the same thing at one and the same time —
this never reaches logical coherence.
Origination (<s>utpāda</s>) is the coming-into-being of what did not exist before;
destruction (<s>vināśa</s>) is the opposite of that;
and permanence (<s>dhrauvya</s>) is that which is devoid of both —
how can they be in one thing at one time?
And the grief, joy, and equanimity
that were cited as proof —
that too is improper, for they are considered
to be caused by latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>).
Moreover, for the proponent of <s>syādvāda</s>,
no definite ascertainment (<s>niścaya</s>) is ever possible,
since both independently and dependently,
the means of knowledge is not a means of knowledge — which itself is a means of knowledge.
One in <s>saṃsāra</s> is also not in <s>saṃsāra</s>;
one who is liberated (<s>mukta</s>) is also not that very one —
due to having and not having that form,
everything is entirely indeterminate.
They [the Jains] reply: The origination of a crown
does not share the property of destruction of the pot;
it is neither other than gold, nor entirely the same —
therefore, the three are not mutually contradictory.
And origination and decay do not lack existence
like permanence, since they are known through cognition.
If those two did not exist, then permanence
could not in truth be a valid cognition either.
Nor is permanence non-existent either,
since it is known without contradiction.
And if this cognition were erroneous,
there would be no non-erroneous cognition in the world.
Origination (<s>utpāda</s>) is the coming-into-being of what did not exist before,
having the character of a different cause;
with the connection of such cognition,
destruction (<s>vināśa</s>) is the opposite of that.
Likewise, permanence (<s>dhrauvya</s>) is said to be
that whose nature is the substrate of both.
Otherwise, if the triad were absent,
why would it not be in one thing at one time?
In one and the same thing, at one and the same time,
all three are thus established.
This is logical, because they have distinct grounds (<s>nimitta</s>);
if they were not distinct, it would not be tenable.
And what is accepted by others through delusion,
namely, that a thing endures for a moment,
in the absence of one of the two,
the reality of that would not hold.
If mere existence is what is accepted,
then that is thus undifferentiated —
the nature of momentary duration
cannot be without origination and decay.
That it is thus already existent —
this can never be established with certainty.
And cessation after having existed is also destruction,
but 'it is that very thing' — this is not the worldly [understanding].
And as for what was declared —
that grief and so forth are caused by latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>) —
that is untenable, since those impressions are variegated
and can never be without a basis.
Due to the impossibility of anything other than constant absence,
and due to the oneness of the entity,
if that [vāsanā] existed, over-extension and the like
would necessarily follow.
'A means of knowledge is not a means of knowledge' —
and the total absence of certainty that was stated —
that too is untenable,
since it is based on one-sidedness (<s>ekānta</s>).
'That means of knowledge is indeed a means of knowledge' —
perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) and inference (<s>laiṅgika</s>) are not refuted.
If those are indeed means of knowledge,
how could it be so without their existence?
It is neither its own existence nor another's non-existence,
due to the contradiction of being both existent and non-existent.
By the same reasoning as its own existence and non-existence,

children.text: na ca nāsty eva tatra tat
children.translated_text: it is not the case that it absolutely does not exist there.
If one says this is merely conceptually constructed,

children.text: na tv itthaṃ tattvato na tat
children.translated_text: and not so in reality,
then what fault is there? If one objects,
then the connection with that [reality] is not established.
Therefore, precisely from the standpoint of <s>anekānta</s> (non-absolutism),
through the proper establishment of means of knowledge,
for the proponent of <s>syādvāda</s>, necessarily,
the highest certainty (<s>niścaya</s>) is established.
By this, everything that was said —
'all is thus' — has been refuted.
For the instruction of disciples, however,
something more is stated.
If the one in <s>saṃsāra</s> is that very same one,
how is liberation (<s>mukti</s>) possible?
And if the liberated one is that very same one,
the designation [of liberation] would be baseless.
That one who is freed from <s>saṃsāra</s>
is called 'liberated' (<s>mukta</s>) —
this is not possible
without that very one having that state.
And if that very one attains that state,
then an entity having the nature of both cessation [of bondage] and its opposite,
like <s>dravya</s> (substance) and <s>paryāya</s> (mode), is an entity that
is necessarily established.
One is ashamed of childhood conduct
who is indeed no longer a child,
and a youth is not ashamed [of youthful conduct] — nor does another person
act with regard to those [childhood actions] in the future.
He is indeed a youth and also an old man,
and the action is not for another's purpose.
An entity consisting of continuity (<s>anvaya</s>) and the like —
in its absence, things would be otherwise.
Continuity (<s>anvaya</s>) and distinction (<s>vyatireka</s>)
are designated as <s>dravya</s> (substance) and <s>paryāya</s> (mode).
Through mutual pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>), differences arise,
and the entity exists through the operation of difference.
Mutual pervasion is not tenable in absolute
difference or in absolute identity,
due to over-extension, due to identity,
and due to the impossibility of meaning of words.
'Mutual' denotes difference,
and 'pervasion' denotes the opposite [i.e., identity].
Therefore, mutual pervasion is possible
only in difference-cum-identity.
Thus, when this is not contrary to reason,
the raising of contradictions by people
merely reveals either perversity
or dullness of intellect.
Contradiction in the proper sense is that which arises
from reasoning — that is called contradiction here.
Just as in absolute difference and so forth,
where those two [difference and identity] themselves are not established.
Clay as <s>dravya</s> (substance) is not the lump, etc.,
devoid of other properties;
nor is that [lump, etc.] ever apprehended anywhere
as released from that [clay substance] alone.
Therefore, that [substance in isolation] is non-existent; likewise, by reasoning,
the one [entity] is established by both.
Hence, the contradiction [of absolute separation]
is characterized by reduction to non-existence.
And in this [view] which is of a different logical category,
the fault of infinite regress and the like does not apply,
due to the determinateness of the distinguishing factor,
and because difference, etc., in isolation is impossible.
Neither does identity devoid of difference exist,
nor difference devoid of identity —
neither exists in isolation; therefore,
what room is there for speculative alternatives?
In what form is there difference?
Is it that very thing, or are they two?
Since what is in isolation is non-existent here,
and since the existent has been described,
and since that entity is known through valid cognition
as having a dual nature,
the speculation about infinite regress and the like
amounts to mere genus-reasoning.
Thus, faults such as 'both defects' and so forth
are not actually refutations,
since difference and identity are properly established
as belonging to a different logical category.
By this, what was stated
by earlier teachers (<s>pūrvasūri</s>) is rejected —
those who, abandoning direct experience, through delusion,
followed mere genus-reasoning.
If <s>dravya</s> (substance) and <s>paryāya</s> (mode) are different,
one thing cannot have both natures;
if identical, let it be considered how
the elimination of either of the two could occur.
That whose elimination does not result
in the elimination of this — that is because
What is different is invariably observed [to be so],
just as a crab [is different] from a camel.
A mode (<s>paryāya</s>) ceases, but not the substance (<s>dravya</s>); therefore that [substance]

children.text: na tu dravyaṃ tato na saḥ
children.translated_text: is not [entirely] different — from the standpoint of substance, [when there is] non-difference,
there is no cessation, just as [there is no cessation] of its own essential nature (<s>svarūpa</s>).
And what is excluded from [the standpoint of] difference —
the position of difference is indeed something else entirely;
and what has been refuted [is the absolute view of] difference.
Through the alternatives of difference and non-difference,
alas, [the entity] has the nature of a different category (<s>jātyantara</s>).
And how could those defects apply to this [entity]
which has the nature of a different category?
For those [defects] which are established in difference and non-difference
are [applicable only] where the categories are absolutely distinct.
Something necessarily ceases;
and of that too, there is something else that does not [cease] in that way.
Therefore, here there is indeed difference of that [entity],
for how else [could there be] cessation and so forth?
The [objection] that 'of that' by the force of syntactic connection
implies 'difference only' is refuted.
'Of that' [means] in an undivided location —
it is said thus through the pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>) of that.
Therefore, the statement 'there is indeed difference of that'
is contrary to [direct] cognition.
And because of that very [entity] being so [i.e., having that nature],
it has the nature of cessation of that and of the other.
Without continuity (<s>anuvṛtti</s>) and cessation (<s>nivṛtti</s>),
nothing whatsoever is established.
For that very [entity] has that nature —
let this be contemplated with subtle intelligence.
When that very [entity] has that nature,
since that very [entity] is so,
therefore no defect whatsoever
applies to our [position].
And this investigation, proceeding thus
through positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>),
establishes that nature [of things],
because the entity has that as its own nature (<s>svabhāva</s>).
Nor does [the doctrine of] difference serve to refute
the <s>anekāntavādin</s> (proponent of manifoldness),
since the entity is held to be of the nature of a different category,
both eternal and non-eternal.
And this is ascertained thus
by the force of recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>).
And this [recognition] is indeed well-established in common experience —
'this is that very [thing]' — in the world.
And it is not proper, without valid reasoning,
to [deny] the transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>) of that [entity],
because of the difference of time and other [factors], and because
of the difference of the entity and the arrival at such [a state].
In absolute oneness, what is manifold [could not exist];
and in [absolute] manifoldness, even that [unity could not exist].
Therefore, how could there be the nature of that?
That is this — having the nature of both.
When that very [entity] has that nature,
through some connection with difference,
since the knower (<s>pramātṛ</s>) also has that nature,
[recognition] is proper in the primary sense.
Even when there is difference, this cognition of the individual (<s>vyakti</s>)
is not consistent through a permanent single connection.
'That is here' — by [unwanted] consequence;
'that is this very [thing]' — is unjustified.
[Recognition] based on similarity and ignorance is logically possible,
but not through the force of error alone.
This is proper when both are not apprehended,
but the postulation of similarity [alone] is not [valid].
Nor is there ever a real refutation even from an erroneous [cognition],
precisely because of the absence [of a real object].
In the case of <s>yogin</s>'s cognition having that nature,
there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge) whatsoever [to refute it].
A <s>yogin</s> cognizes manifoldness;
[the objection] 'not manifold' has no valid cognition here.
Because of the teaching (<s>deśanā</s>) proceeding
in accordance with those to be guided (<s>vineya</s>).
And the [recognition] that is observed
in cut and regrown nails, hair, grass, and such —
that too is merely an appearance of that,
not the very same [thing].
Even when there is a semblance of perception (<s>pratyakṣābhāsa</s>),
just as [it] is not a non-<s>pramāṇa</s>,
so too this should be understood as perception,
a valid means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>).
Since this is a variety of <s>matijñāna</s> (sensory knowledge),
it is not undesirable.
By the force of this, therefore, [the doctrine of]
the eternal-and-non-eternal nature and so forth of entities is established.
Eighth <s>Stabaka</s> (Chapter)
(1) Refutation of the <s>Brahma</s>-<s>Advaita</s> (non-dualism) doctrine
Others, however, maintain non-duality (<s>advaita</s>)
through the investigation of pure being (<s>sat</s>), <s>Brahman</s>, and so forth.
What differentiates being (<s>sat</s>) is nothing other [than being itself],
and that is merely that [being] alone.
Just as a person afflicted by an eye-disease (<s>timira</s>)
[perceives] the pure sky (<s>ākāśa</s>)
as if mixed with different
specks, [and] imagines [it to be so],
so this pure <s>Brahman</s>,
which is beyond conceptual construction (<s>nirvikalpa</s>), through <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance)
appears as if having attained impurity,
manifesting in the form of difference.
Here too, others say thus:
<s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) is not separate from being (<s>sat</s>);
and that is merely that [being] alone —
hence the appearance of difference is without basis.
If that [<s>avidyā</s>] itself, though of the nature of non-difference,
is the basis for the appearance of difference,
this cannot be ascertained
without a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge).
And even if a <s>pramāṇa</s> exists,
since it is distinct from the object of knowledge (<s>prameya</s>),
would it not be the case that non-duality (<s>advaita</s>) itself [is undermined]?
And in the absence of that [distinction], it is without <s>pramāṇa</s>.
And through the distinction of <s>vidyā</s> (knowledge) and <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) and so forth,
[the doctrine] is refuted by its own independence [i.e., internal contradictions].
And through the application of doubt and so forth regarding that,
and through cognition — let this be considered.
Others offer this explanation
for establishing the doctrine of equal existence (<s>samabhāva</s>):
the teaching of non-duality (<s>advaita</s>) is prescribed in scripture
but not in the ultimate sense (<s>tattvataḥ</s>).
And this cannot be refuted by reasoning,
because of the established authority of valid scripture and so forth,
and because of the existence of <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence) and <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation),
and the accomplishment of effort for that purpose.
Otherwise, if non-duality (<s>advaita</s>) were the ultimate truth,
alas, [with respect to] <s>saṃsāra</s> and <s>mokṣa</s>,
the futility of all religious practice
would undesirably follow.
Ninth <s>Stabaka</s> (Chapter)

children.text: (1)mokṣa kī saṃbhāvanā tathā mokṣa ke sādhana
children.translated_text: (1) The possibility of <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation) and the means to <s>mokṣa</s>
Yet others say thus:
<s>mokṣa</s> (liberation) simply does not exist,
either because of the absence of means [to it], or
it is not always [available] to all embodied beings.
If that [liberation] depends on the maturation of <s>karma</s> and so forth,
then, since <s>karma</s> and so forth are beginningless,
how could such maturation
and so forth [ever come about]?
Because that [<s>karma</s>] itself has manifold forms,
it is not proper [to say] 'that is always so.'
The supreme state of that [soul],
which has arisen manifold times indeed —
here too, others explain:
there exists a means [consisting of] right view (<s>darśana</s>) and so forth
to the reality of liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>),
the supreme [means] declared by the omniscient one (<s>sarvajña</s>).
Right view (<s>darśana</s>), the seed of liberation,
<s>samyaktva</s> (right faith), knowledge of reality (<s>tattvavedana</s>) —
the ender of suffering, the beginning of bliss —
these are declared as its synonyms.
For one who has the beginningless nature of being capable of liberation (<s>bhavya</s>),
through connection with that essential nature,
when the supreme and other [conditions] are past
in the durations of <s>karma</s> —
that one attains right view (<s>darśana</s>),
having pierced through the terrible knot of <s>karma</s> (<s>karmagranthi</s>)
by a wholesome disposition —
at some time, some [rare being] indeed.
And when this [right view] is present, that blessed one,
endowed with right view (<s>samyagdarśana</s>),
whose soul is purified by faith in the truths (<s>tattvaśraddhāna</s>),
does not delight in the ocean of worldly existence (<s>bhavodadhi</s>).
He perceives with the eye of the intellect (<s>buddhicakṣus</s>)
the true nature of this [reality],
in accordance with correct scripture (<s>samyakśāstra</s>),
like one whose eye disease has been cured.
Having seen that, he reflects thus
with a serene inner self,
on the nature of existence as it truly is,
having attained supreme detachment (<s>saṃvega</s>):
Afflicted by birth, death, old age, disease,
illness, grief, and other calamities —
solely for the suffering of beings,
ah, this terrible great ocean [of existence]!
But <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation) is for supreme happiness,
free from the afflictions of birth and so forth,
liberated from the power of fear,
always free from obstacles.
The cause of worldly existence is violence (<s>hiṃsā</s>) and so forth,
as seen from the positive concomitance with suffering and so forth.
But the cause of liberation is non-violence (<s>ahiṃsā</s>) and so forth,
because of the cessation of obstacles.
Having thus understood the worthlessness of worldly existence
and the virtuous nature of liberation,
one whose soul is purified strives constantly
for that purpose, in accordance with scripture (<s>āgama</s>).
That one performs difficult (<s>duṣkara</s>) austerities
that are [too hard for] beings of little courage,
because of firm devotion to liberation,
like a lover in the presence of a beautiful woman.
Whatever does not properly accomplish
a particular desirable end —
that practice pains the mind,
because it obstructs the attainment of that [goal].
Therefore, that [practice] is not truly difficult
when properly considered.
Rather, what is difficult by reason
is that which accomplishes what is to be rejected.
Just as a person afflicted by disease,
tasting even a morsel of health,
being wise, even in a painful treatment,
proceeds steadily with proper satisfaction,
so too should the noblest of persons (<s>narottama</s>) be understood,
seized by the disease of <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence),
having obtained a trace of the health of tranquility (<s>śama</s>),
truly [engaging] in the treatment for that.
And thus proceeding,
with firm resolve according to one's ability,
having attained pure conduct (<s>cāritra</s>),
one gradually attains absolute [knowledge] (<s>kevala</s>).
Then, having become omniscient (<s>sarvavid</s>),
having brought about the destruction of <s>karma</s>
that sustains worldly existence, through the yoga of knowledge (<s>jñānayoga</s>),
one attains eternal <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation).
The yoga of knowledge (<s>jñānayoga</s>) is pure <s>tapas</s> (austerity) —
thus and so forth has been declared.
The intended meaning
of that is stated [as follows]:
The supreme culmination of <s>jñānayoga</s> (the yoga of knowledge)
has been declared by the lords of <s>yogins</s>
to be the steadfastness called <s>śaileśī</s> (rock-like immobility).
From that, liberation — without doubt.
And <s>dharma</s> (righteousness), being the nature of the self,
grants liberation because it is the means of purification.
It is imperishable, because it cannot be lost,
since it always abides thus in liberation.
And the transformation of conduct (<s>cāritra</s>)
does not cease in every respect,
since in the scripture one who is liberated (<s>siddha</s>) is described
as neither possessing conduct nor otherwise.
Nor is the cessation of that [conduct] justified here
through the cessation of [a particular] state,
just as when the prescribed time is exceeded,
the state of being liberated (<s>siddha</s>) [continues] there indeed.
Therefore, liberation through <s>jñānayoga</s> (the yoga of knowledge)
is properly established.
If this is stated in accordance with other systems (<s>tantrāntara</s>),
it does not create a fault.
Tenth <s>Stabaka</s> (Chapter)
(1) Refutation of the <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s>'s denial of omniscience (<s>sarvajñatā</s>)
Here too, others assert:
an omniscient being (<s>sarvajña</s>) simply does not exist,
because there is no valid cognition (<s>pramā</s>) that can apprehend such [a being] —
thus [say] those who follow reasoning (<s>nyāya</s>).
By the <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge) of perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>),
no omniscient being is apprehended.
Nor is there any invariable concomitant mark (<s>liṅga</s>)
by which [the existence of an omniscient being could be inferred].
Nor through scripture (<s>āgama</s>), since that [scripture]
is a conveyor of injunctions (<s>vidhi</s>) and so forth.
Because of not being perceptible,
[an omniscient being] cannot be known even through <s>upamāna</s> (analogy).
Nor through <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption), since everything
is established even without that [omniscient being].
Since the five <s>pramāṇas</s> do not apply,
there the <s>pramāṇa</s> of non-existence (<s>abhāva</s>) is [to be invoked].
The determination of <s>dharma</s> (duty) and <s>adharma</s> (non-duty), however,
[comes] from scripture called the <s>Veda</s>,
since that is authorless (<s>apauruṣeya</s>)
and free from the defects of [human] authorship.
And [the <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s>] says: when the <s>Veda</s>,
like a lamp, is common to all,
and <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> are known [from it],
for what purpose is a [omniscient] person postulated?
The distinction of <s>iṣṭa</s> (Vedic sacrifice) and <s>pūrta</s> (charitable works) and so forth
is established for all people from this [<s>Veda</s>],
well-known through common usage,
just like days and so forth.
What is given in the inner altar (<s>antarvedī</s>)
by the priests (<s>ṛtvij</s>), with <s>mantra</s>-consecrations,
in the presence of <s>brāhmaṇas</s> —
that is called <s>iṣṭa</s> (sacrifice).
Wells, cisterns, tanks,
temples of deities,
and the gift of food —
this is called <s>pūrta</s> (charitable works).
And beyond this, whatever pure conduct
of a great-souled one free from desires —
<s>dhyāna</s> (meditation) and so forth, which yields the fruit of liberation —
that is called <s>śreyas</s> (the highest good).
And the entire system of <s>varṇas</s> (social classes) and <s>āśramas</s> (life-stages)
is indeed derived from that [<s>Veda</s>].
There is no need whatsoever
for one who sees supersensory objects (<s>atīndriyārthadraṣṭṛ</s>).
Here too, some proponents of omniscience (<s>sarvajñavādin</s>)
respond thus:
how can the non-application of the five <s>pramāṇas</s>
be established in that case?
If perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) has all objects as its domain,
then that itself creates the negation [of the omniscient being].
How can there be non-existence of this [omniscient being]?
If not, then the same [argument applies] here too.
And <s>dharma</s> and so forth are also perceptible,
because they are objects of knowledge, like a pot and so forth.
For someone, everything indeed [is perceptible] —
hence inference is not non-existent [as a proof].
From scripture (<s>āgama</s>) too, the establishment of that [omniscient being is possible],
since that [scripture] is the result of [valid] injunction (<s>codanā</s>).
And the validity of that [scripture] is intrinsic (<s>svataḥ</s>),
and its eternality is like that of <s>śruti</s> (Vedic revelation).
Through the definitive resolution of all doubts
residing in the heart, in apprehending that [omniscient being],
and in the apprehension of <s>upamāna</s> (analogy) there —
not otherwise, and not elsewhere either.
Through <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption) too, the supersensory reach
of scripture can be known,
for otherwise, no confidence in that [scripture]
arises for one in the state of delusion (<s>chadmastha</s>).
Thus, the non-application of the five <s>pramāṇas</s>
is not justified in that case.
Nevertheless, [to claim] the validity of non-existence (<s>abhāva</s>) [as proof] —
that is the bluster of the blind led by the blind.
That the establishment of <s>dharma</s> and so forth from the <s>Veda</s>
can be properly understood, alas, without
one who sees the supersensory —
from where [does this claim come]? Let it be considered.
Not through the tradition of elders (<s>vṛddhasampradāya</s>),
because of its being cut off at the root.
Nor does the <s>Cārvāka</s> (materialist) [accept it], since from that [perspective]
supersensory objects cannot be ascertained.
The validity [of the <s>Veda</s>] regarding matters of form [i.e., perceptible things]
does not justify [its validity regarding] tradition [i.e., imperceptible matters],
just as [the testimony of] those blind from birth [is unreliable] —
let this be examined here as well.
The equivalence of the meaning of that [<s>Veda</s>]
with worldly objects
cannot be ascertained in other [domains],
because of the observation of the contrary regarding that.
If something is otherworldly (<s>alaukika</s>) because of [the <s>Veda</s>'s]
eternality and authorlessness (<s>apauruṣeyatva</s>),
then the doubt regarding that [extends] elsewhere too —
for the wise person, it does not cease.
And there is no means to remove that [doubt]
without one who perceives the supersensory.
And having considered this, it was well stated
by <s>Dharmakīrti</s>:
One knows the meaning for oneself, [being subject to] passion and so forth;
the <s>Veda</s> does not [convey its meaning] from another [source].
The <s>Veda</s> itself does not communicate [its meaning] —
whence then the understanding of the <s>Veda</s>'s meaning?
Therefore, in the <s>śruti</s> (Vedic revelation) [that says] 'one desiring heaven
should offer the <s>agnihotra</s> (fire sacrifice),'
and 'one should eat dog's flesh' —
what valid cognition is there that 'this is not the [intended] meaning'?
If [one says] that the word [of the <s>Veda</s>], like a lamp,
is a revealer of meaning by its own power (<s>svataḥ</s>),
there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge)
for this [claim] either.
And contrary illumination
certainly occurs sometimes.
For thus a lamp [shining on] a blue lotus
illuminates [it as having] redness.
Therefore, without qualification,
cognition does not arise [from words alone].
If [cognition] depends on convention (<s>saṅketa</s>),
then [the claim of validity] 'by its own power alone' is unjustified.
Whether the convention is valid or not —
this doubt does not cease.
And because of the apprehension of its diversity,
due to adherence to one's own predisposition.
The interpretation of the <s>apauruṣeya</s> (authorless scripture) too
is not tenable, due to the absence of a valid means of knowledge;
and because of mutual contradiction,
and because the excellence and such qualities of that are uncertain.
The ascertainment of its excellence is not established
by the agreement of other means of knowledge;
that is not justifiable for what is beyond the senses,
because of the contradiction with the respective natures of those.
Therefore, this interpretation of it
is merely a declaration of one's own intent;
is it not equal to the word of <s>Jaimini</s> and others —
what difference does another statement make for you?
"This is a post, that is the path" —
one person says this here;
another says "I myself declare" —
let the difference between the two be examined.
Nor does the <s>apauruṣeya</s> (authorless) nature of that
hold up well upon proper reasoning,
because in the absence of the activity of a speaker,
those words would not be apprehended.
If there is the activity of a speaker,
then in its presence, is it not worldly?
You hold the speech to be <s>apauruṣeya</s> (authorless)
with regard to the substance of the words.
And even in what is seen, the doubt
arising from an unseen agent
does not cease
without one who sees supersensory objects.
"This cognition arises from sin, not from merit" — this is not a valid means of knowledge,
for the world does not ascertain this
due to the multiplicity of conflicting views
and the uncertainty regarding their prevalence.
Because even many people may be deluded
and thus engage in false conduct,
and because there is no contradiction with the number of valid means —
how can this be asserted thus?
But if a certain person who sees supersensory objects
is accepted,
then even such a conception of things
would be within the range of possibility.
Moreover, its <s>apauruṣeya</s> (authorless) nature
is not known from any other source,
due to faults such as the deviation
of non-remembrance of the author and the like.
Even through repetition and such practices,
the author is not unknown;
indeed, <s>Aṣṭaka</s> and others are remembered
by those who know.
Repetition of actions, truly,
produces proficiency;
even for one who has himself composed a study,
that state is not contradicted.
And the non-disclosure
may be for the purpose of establishing authority.
The efficacy of <s>mantras</s> and the like,
even of the <s>Śabara</s> (tribal) ones, is clearly
recognized in the entire world,
yet that too is not invariable.
In the <s>Veda</s> too, this great soul
is recited in various places;
and by a valid means of knowledge, one cannot say
that this is non-existent.
Nor is the imagination of a subject matter
greater merely because it concerns supersensory things;
for one who does not see directly there,
it is entirely like a blind person regarding form.
For from the scripture revealed by the <s>sarvajña</s> (omniscient one),
which encompasses all objects, this supreme
determination of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>
is established, and from no other source anywhere.
2. Refutation of the refutation of omniscience
Here too, another wise one
speaks thus, a well-said statement:
"This desired object could be known
if that superiority were possible."
"Is this so or not?" — another says:
"Whether it has faults or faultlessness,
it is difficult to ascertain
due to the difficulty of obtaining valid means." Thus others know.
Here too, the elders say:
"Established and invariable
is the knowledge in the world of the qualities and such of great souls,
in a general way."
"The apprehension of their conduct and such
is otherwise unreasonable;
and particular knowledge too, in this way —
is it not likewise from practice?"
"From the observed diminution of faults here,
the possibility of their complete destruction arises;
and when that is established, the wise know
that this is his superiority."
"From the power of resolving all doubts
seated in the heart,
and when the present is at hand,
from the non-contradiction of the objects revealed by him."
"And even though he is not seen now,
it is not the non-existence of sovereignty itself;
its possibility, justified by reasoning,
has already been demonstrated."
"Even now, the intuitive insight
regarding supersensory matters
of skilled physicians, ascetics, and the like
is seen to be non-deceptive."
"Thus in that case too, when that state exists,
there is no contradiction whatsoever;
from the non-contradiction of the objects revealed by him,
and from the existence of knowledge at present."
"In everything seen, from agreement,
doubt of deception does not arise
regarding the knower in what is unseen,
from the apprehension of his superiority."
"Even by the nature of reality, that
would not be deceptive;
'as each successive [perspective], so the seeing' —
this is not the current view."
"If a valid means of knowledge is thus established,
then what here is not a valid means?
For there is not a single untruthful statement
in a person who speaks much."
"Since not one statement is untruthful,
but rather everything is as heard —
that scripture in which valid knowledge resides
is accepted by the wise as authoritative."
"The self exists, the named is distinct, <s>karma</s> exists,
from the conjunction of those arises becoming, and otherwise
<s>mokṣa</s> (liberation); <s>hiṃsā</s> (violence) and the like are primary [sins],
and their cessation together with its means —"
"Agreement with supersensory objects,
a purified method of meditation,
where all this is consistent —
that which is revealed by the <s>yogin</s> is the [true] scripture."
"And even one who is qualified for this
but is himself ignorant —
when he becomes a knower of what has been taught, he is wise;
its purposelessness is otherwise."
"From the teaching of the means of attaining
the qualities such as knowledge of others' minds and the paths,
this too encompasses all objects" —
thus is the establishment of its nature.
Chapter Eleven
1. Refutation of the refutation of the word-meaning relation
Others declare here,
who have labored on the path of reasoning:
"There is no real relation between word and meaning
in the nature of things."
"There is no identity, because of the consequence of the non-existence of duality,
and because of the difference in cognitions;
because of the consequence of cutting the mouth and such
when weapons are applied — it stands by convention."
"Because the object is not present,
and because of otherwise-speaking when that is seen,
and because of the compulsion of other cognitions —
its origination too does not hold."
"If words referred exclusively to ultimate particulars,
there would be no binding;
there could be no application to objects
that differ according to different philosophical views."
"And regarding what is past and what is not yet born,
no speech would be untrue" —
this position is held to be
the Buddhist view of meaning.
"The denotable is thus <s>apoha</s> (exclusion),
not a real universal;
because of its inapplicability without distinction
from others, since it stands thus."
"And when this exists, what need of anything else,
since from the word there is cognition of what possesses that?
In the absence of that, there is no possession of that;
since it is erroneous — is it not so?"
"But in the view of a non-erroneous universal,
there is no movement from the staff to the staff-bearer;
when there is confusion of both in what possesses that —
your view from difference is not like that either."
Others state thus:
"Characterized by the expressible and the expressive,
there is a connection between word and meaning,
because from that there is the cognition of that, and so on."
"This is not so, because by the differentiation
of making the seen and the conceptualized into one;
and because of the absence of a single cognizer,
the reality of those two is not established."
"From the word arises an awareness of the impression of that,
and from that the conceptual cognition —
this is what we say;
the non-establishment of that does not follow from that."
"The awareness born of impressions is distinct,
and that never arises
from another, because of equal timing and the like;
for there is no distinction of another."
"Because of being already produced and because of non-existence,
the arising of another from both does not occur;
without a distinguishing material cause,
how can that have that nature?"
"For as stated, from its own cause
destruction with a cause could occur;
such a fabrication by reasoning —
for this very reason it is not justified."
"And since identity and such are not accepted here,
the faults arising therefrom
do not apply to us; nor do other faults,
because of the difference in that, from the difference in causes."
"Just as the distinction of <s>Rāma</s> and others
from the children of barren women and such exists,
so too the distinction of true and false words and the like
exists from the difference in their causes."
"Even though words refer exclusively to ultimate particulars,
the attribution of the fault of others
has been refuted;
let this be properly considered."
"The fault of another is never logically applicable
to someone else by reasoning;
the non-description by the <s>Buddhas</s>
is not like that of a mendicant, of a tribesman, and such."
"The distinction of that is known,
as between a valid means and a non-valid means,
from the examination of its intrinsic nature and such,
and likewise from observation in the world."
"And the disregard of convention here,
without the destruction and subsidence of those [karmas],
being the doer of that, bears fruit
for <s>yogins</s>, but does not exist otherwise."
"Because words have the nature of expressing everything,
due to their manifold powers;
and the expressible likewise in another context —
the term <s>nāga</s> applies even in his convention."
"A thing has infinite properties,
and only some property of it
is expressed, not all —
therefore this is not a refutation."
"What is grasped by the senses is one thing,
and the domain of words is another;
from a word, one with different senses understands,
but does not see directly."
"In one way, from the contact with burning,
one who is burned conceives of burning;
in another way, through the word 'burning,'
the meaning of burning is understood."
"The expressible is different from what is grasped by the senses,
and it does not cause burning;
yet from the establishment of non-difference from difference
in such cognition — that is reality for us."
"The denotability of <s>apoha</s> (exclusion) too
is not established by reasoning,
because of its non-existence, and because it too
is cognized by the mind through the distinction of real things."
"All <s>saṃskāras</s> (conditioned formations) are momentary" —
otherwise this is contradicted;
<s>apoha</s> (exclusion) is not a <s>saṃskāra</s>,
and it is not accepted as momentary.
"And thus the reality of things
is, alas, not ascertained from scripture;
and in its absence, clearly
this amounts to a refutation of mere chaff."
"Even in the non-description by the <s>Buddha</s>, there is no fault;
and in praise too, there is no merit;
invocation and non-apprehension and the like
are certain from the non-relation of word and meaning."

children.text: (2) jñāna tathā kiryā ke bīca prādhānya-aprādhānya kā praśna
children.translated_text: (2) The question of the primacy and non-primacy of knowledge and action
Some desire attainment necessarily
from knowledge alone;
others from action alone;
yet others, the discerning, from both.
"Knowledge indeed is fruit-bearing for people,
action is not considered fruit-bearing,
because for one who engages through false knowledge,
attainment of the fruit is impossible."
"And those in the world who are devoid of knowledge
are seen performing great actions —
they labor for an exceedingly long time,
devoted to affliction and exertion."
"And those possessing knowledge, by its power,
in their respective fields of action,
through connection with superior fruits,
are happy even with little action."
"And in the state of <s>kevalajñāna</s> (absolute knowledge),
liberation too is not otherwise;
even with any amount of effort through action,
therefore it is considered to come from knowledge."
"Action alone is fruit-bearing for people,
knowledge is not considered fruit-bearing;
for one who knows about women, food, and pleasures
does not become happy merely from knowledge."
"And those in the world who are devoid of action
are seen, even though possessing knowledge,
to be objects of pity for others,
bereft of happiness and prosperity."
"And those endowed with action, through that connection,
from the state of exalted fruit,
even fools, for the most part,
are masters over the learned, and blameless."
"And from the connection with the excellence of action,
liberation of the <s>kevalin</s> (omniscient one) too is achieved;
otherwise, even in the state of omniscience,
that does not occur — therefore it is dependent on that."
"All fruit is accomplished
through the combination of knowledge and action;
and the existence of those two
is ultimately not otherwise."
"If, having fully understood the object to be accomplished,
one rightly engages,
then one indeed accomplishes that —
and thus <s>Bṛhaspati</s> has said:"
"Right engagement is called
the means for attaining what is to be accomplished;
if that is not attained, the status of being a means
does not apply to it."
"Therefore, one who undertakes what cannot be accomplished
never has right knowledge;
and one who does not undertake what can be accomplished" —
the two are mutually connected.
"Therefore, the action of one who knows scripture
is called [true] action;
and one who knows scripture
engages in that to the best of his ability."
"One who knows the true nature of the wish-fulfilling gem
is not afflicted by misfortune;
when there are various means for its attainment,
he does not engage elsewhere, leaving that aside."
"And one who engages elsewhere
does not truly know its nature;
the bee who knows the fragrance of the jasmine cluster
does not delight in <s>darbha</s> grass."
"And liberation arises precisely from the excellence of
<s>kevalajñāna</s> (absolute knowledge) and action;
its existence follows from the existence of those,
and its absence from their absence."
"The two are not properly separated" —
this is accepted by others too;
because of the inability to accomplish their own purpose [separately] —
as the great sage <s>Vyāsa</s> has said:
"A wrestler who is also an ascetic,
and a warrior who has never been wounded,
a woman who drinks liquor yet claims chastity —
O King, in these I do not believe."
(3) The nature of liberation
Liberation here is freedom from death and the like,
through the exhaustion of <s>karma</s>;
without <s>karma</s> there is no birth anywhere,
as stated by the ancient teachers.
Just as when a seed is burned,
no sprout ever appears,
so when the seed of <s>karma</s> is burned,
the sprout of existence does not grow.
In the absence of birth, old age and death
are absent, due to the absence of their cause;
and in their absence, the complete
absence of suffering exists forever.
And the state of supreme bliss
in their absence is eternal,
established through the absence of affliction —
the happiness of the <s>siddhas</s> (perfected ones) is thus accepted.
Free from all pairs of opposites,
devoid of all afflictions,
having accomplished all perfect results —
what can be said of their happiness?
Formless, knowing all things,
dwelling above the three worlds,
with attachments destroyed, great souls —
they ever abide in bliss.
Having heard these discussions,
the wise person, contemplating them,
comprehends the intended meaning
of the treatises presented herein.
Seven hundred verses
in the <s>anuṣṭubh</s> metre have been composed —
by <s>Ācārya Haribhadra</s>,
the <s>Śāstravārtāsamuccaya</s> (Compendium of Discussions on the Sciences).

children.translated_text: Having composed this treatise, whatever merit has been obtained by me herein,

children.text: bhavavirahabījam anaghaṃ labhatāṃ bhavyo janas tena //
children.translated_text: may the worthy beings attain through that the faultless seed of freedom from worldly existence.

children.text: yaṃ buddhaṃ bodhayantaḥ śikhijalamarutas tuṣṭuvur lokavṛttyai
children.translated_text: That <s>Buddha</s> whom fire, water, and wind, awakening him, praised for the welfare of the world,
in whom knowledge arose that was the cause of destroying the darkness pervading the worlds,
whose skill in speech is blessed with the transformation into the own languages of all living beings —
in that supreme lord of gods, the blessed one, may devotion and love be cultivated by you.
